lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • At dynamic equilibrium the amounts of liquid water and water vapour become constant because the forward and reverse rates are equal.
  • A reversible reaction proceeds in the forward and reverse direction and does not go to completion.
  • Kc is the ratio of the two rate constants, Kc = k1/k2.
  • For A + B <=> C + D, Kc = [C][D] / [A][B].
  • A very small Kc, such as 10^-30 for N2 + O2 <=> 2NO, means the forward reaction does not proceed appreciably.
  • For PCl5 <=> PCl3 + Cl2, the unit of Kc is mol / dm^3.
  • When Kc = 1, the reaction is 50% complete.
  • The law of mass action states that the rate of a reaction is proportional to the product of the active masses of the reacting substances.

Solved Exercises

Exercise 1 — Choose the correct answers from the given options

Q: i. Consider the system: Water(l) <=> Water(g). At dynamic equilibrium:

Options: (a) reversible reaction stops (b) amount of liquid water and water vapour is the same (c) amount of liquid water and water vapour is constant (d) Amount of liquid is minimum

Correct answer: amount of liquid water and water vapour is constant

Q: ii. A reversible reaction proceeds in the:

Options: (a) reverse direction (b) forward direction (c) forward and reverse direction (d) more backward less forward

Correct answer: forward and reverse direction

Q: iii. The equilibrium constant (Kc) is:

Options: (a) The sum of the two rate constants (b) The difference of the two rate constants (c) The ratio of the two rate constants (d) The product of the two rate constants

Correct answer: The ratio of the two rate constants

Q: iv. For the reaction A + B <=> C + D, Kc is equal to:

Options: (a) ([A]+[B]) / ([C]+[D]) (b) ([A]+[D]) / ([B]+[C]) (c) [A][B] / [C][D] (d) [C][D] / [A][B]

Correct answer: [C][D] / [A][B]

Q: v. For a reaction N2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2NO(g), if Kc = 10^-30 at 25°C. One can predict:

Options: (a) More NO is formed (b) The forward reaction goes to completion (c) The backward reaction goes to completion (d) More reactants are consumed

Correct answer: The backward reaction goes to completion

Q: vi. The unit of Kc for the following system is: PCl5 <=> PCl3 + Cl2

Options: (a) mol^2 / L^2 (b) L / mol (c) mol / L^2 (d) mol / dm^3

Correct answer: mol / dm^3

Q: vii. Molecules of chlorine do not decompose into atomic chlorine i.e. Cl2 <=> 2Cl. This is because Kc of this reaction is:

Options: (a) Very large (b) Very small (c) Zero (d) 1

Correct answer: Very small

Q: viii. How much reaction is complete when Kc = 1:

Options: (a) 10% (b) 25% (c) 50% (d) 100%

Correct answer: 50%

options: amount of liquid water and water vapour is constant
amount of liquid water and water vapour is the same
mcqs.why: At dynamic equilibrium the rates of evaporation and condensation become equal, so the amounts of liquid water and water vapour stay constant even though both processes continue.

mcqs.q: ii. A reversible reaction proceeds in the:
mcqs.why: Reversible reactions are defined in the chapter as reactions which proceed in the forward as well as in the reverse direction and do not go to completion.

The sum of the two rate constants
The difference of the two rate constants
The product of the two rate constants
mcqs.why: At equilibrium k1[A][B] = k2[C][D], so Kc = k1/k2. The equilibrium constant is therefore the ratio of the forward and reverse rate constants.

mcqs.q: iv. For the reaction A + B <=> C + D, Kc is equal to:
mcqs.why: Kc is the product of the concentrations of the products divided by the product of the concentrations of the reactants, which here gives [C][D] / [A][B].

mcqs.q: v. For a reaction N2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2NO(g), if Kc = 10^-30 at 25°C. One can predict:
options: The forward reaction goes to completion
The backward reaction goes to completion
mcqs.why: Kc = 10^-30 is extremely small. The chapter states that a very small Kc shows the reaction does not proceed appreciably in the forward direction, so the equilibrium lies far towards the reactants — in effect the backward reaction goes to completion and almost no NO remains at equilibrium.

mcqs.q: vi. The unit of Kc for the following system is: PCl5 <=> PCl3 + Cl2
mcqs.why: Kc = [PCl3][Cl2] / [PCl5]. Two concentration units in the numerator divided by one in the denominator leave one concentration unit, mol/dm^3.

mcqs.q: vii. Molecules of chlorine do not decompose into atomic chlorine i.e. Cl2 <=> 2Cl. This is because Kc of this reaction is:
mcqs.why: A very small value of Kc reflects that the reaction does not proceed appreciably in the forward direction, so Cl2 molecules stay as molecules instead of forming atomic chlorine.

mcqs.q: viii. How much reaction is complete when Kc = 1:
mcqs.why: When Kc = 1, the product of the product concentrations equals the product of the reactant concentrations, so reactants and products are present in equal measure and the reaction is half, that is 50%, complete.

options: The product of the active masses of the reacting substances
The sum of the active masses of the reacting substances
The difference of the active masses of the reacting substances
The product of the active masses of the products only
mcqs.why: The law of mass action, as defined in the chapter, states that the rate of a chemical reaction is proportional to the product of the active masses of the reacting substances.

mcqs.q: In the law of mass action, the term active mass means:
options: The mass of the substance taken, measured in grams
The total volume of the solution, measured in dm^3
The molar concentration, i.e. the number of moles per dm^3 in a dilute solution
The total number of molecules present in the vessel
mcqs.why: The chapter explains that by active mass we mean the molar concentration, that is the number of moles per dm^3 in a dilute solution.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Kc is the product of the concentrations of the products divided by the product of the concentrations of the reactants, each raised to the power of its coefficient.
  • For N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3, Kc = [NH3]^2 / ([N2] [H2]^3).
  • The law of mass action was suggested by Guldberg and Waage in 1864.
  • Active mass means molar concentration, the number of moles per dm^3 in a dilute solution.
  • Kc has no units when the number of moles of reactants and products are equal; for PCl5 <=> PCl3 + Cl2 its unit is mol/dm^3.
  • Reversible reactions proceed in both directions and do not go to completion; irreversible reactions proceed in one direction only and go to completion.
  • Dynamic equilibrium in a closed vessel is the state where the forward and reverse rates are equal and concentrations become constant.

Solved Exercises

Exercise 2 — Write short answers to the following questions

Q: i. Give an expression for Kc for the following reversible reactions. A) N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g) B) H2(g) + CO2(g) <=> CO(g) + H2O(g) C) 4NH3(g) + 5O2(g) <=> 4NO(g) + 6H2O(g)

Ans: The equilibrium constant Kc is the product of the concentrations of the products divided by the product of the concentrations of the reactants, each concentration being raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation.
A) Kc = [NH3]^2 / ([N2] [H2]^3)
B) Kc = [CO] [H2O] / ([H2] [CO2])
C) Kc = [NO]^4 [H2O]^6 / ([NH3]^4 [O2]^5)

Q: ii. Define law of mass action.

Ans: The law of mass action was suggested by two chemists, Guldberg and Waage, in 1864. It states that the rate or speed of a chemical reaction is proportional to the product of the active masses of the reacting substances. By active mass we mean the molar concentration, i.e. the number of moles per dm^3 in a dilute solution.

Q: iii. Write down the units of Kc.

Ans: The unit of Kc depends upon the equilibrium constant expression for the given reaction. If the number of moles of reactants and products are equal, the concentration units cancel out and Kc has no units. If the moles are not equal, Kc has units; for example, for PCl5 <=> PCl3 + Cl2, Kc = [PCl3][Cl2] / [PCl5], so the unit of Kc is mol/dm^3.

Q: iv. What are reversible and irreversible reactions?

Ans: Reversible reactions are those reactions which proceed in the forward as well as in the reverse direction and do not go to completion, e.g. N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3 and H2 + I2 <=> 2HI. Irreversible reactions are those which proceed in one direction only and go to completion, so that the products do not react back to form the reactants.

Q: v. What is dynamic equilibrium?

Ans: Dynamic equilibrium is the state of a reversible reaction in a closed vessel at which the rate of the forward reaction becomes equal to the rate of the reverse reaction. At this stage the concentrations of the reactants and products become constant. It seems that the reaction has stopped, but actually both reactions continue at the same rate, e.g. evaporation and condensation of water in a closed container.

mcqs.q: What is the expression for Kc for the reaction N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g)?
mcqs.why: Each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient: NH3 has coefficient 2 and H2 has coefficient 3, giving Kc = [NH3]^2 / ([N2] [H2]^3).

mcqs.q: What is the expression for Kc for the reaction H2(g) + CO2(g) <=> CO(g) + H2O(g)?
mcqs.why: All coefficients are 1, so Kc is simply the product of the product concentrations divided by the product of the reactant concentrations: [CO] [H2O] / ([H2] [CO2]).

mcqs.q: What is the expression for Kc for the reaction 4NH3(g) + 5O2(g) <=> 4NO(g) + 6H2O(g)?
mcqs.why: The powers are the balanced coefficients: NO is raised to 4, H2O to 6, NH3 to 4 and O2 to 5, giving Kc = [NO]^4 [H2O]^6 / ([NH3]^4 [O2]^5).

mcqs.q: The law of mass action was suggested by:
mcqs.why: The chapter states that the law of mass action was suggested by two chemists, Guldberg and Waage, in 1864.

mcqs.q: According to the law of mass action, the rate of a chemical reaction is proportional to:
options: The sum of the active masses of the reacting substances
The ratio of the active masses of the products to the vessel volume
The product of the active masses of the reacting substances
The active mass of the catalyst used in the reaction
mcqs.why: The law of mass action states that the rate or speed of a chemical reaction is proportional to the product of the active masses of the reacting substances.

mcqs.q: By active mass in the law of mass action we mean:
options: The molar concentration, i.e. the number of moles per dm^3 in a dilute solution
The mass of the substance in grams per vessel
The number of moles of products formed per second
The density of the reacting substance in the mixture
mcqs.why: The chapter defines active mass as the molar concentration, that is the number of moles per dm^3 in a dilute solution.

mcqs.q: Kc has no units when:
options: The number of moles of reactants and products are not equal
The reaction is carried out in an open vessel
A catalyst is added to the reaction mixture
The number of moles of reactants and products are equal
mcqs.why: The chapter states that if the number of moles of reactants and products are equal, the concentration units cancel out and Kc has no units.

mcqs.q: For the reaction PCl5 <=> PCl3 + Cl2, the unit of Kc is:
mcqs.why: Kc = [PCl3][Cl2] / [PCl5], so one concentration unit remains after cancellation, and the chapter gives the unit of Kc for this reaction as mol/dm^3.

mcqs.q: Reversible reactions are those reactions which:
options: Proceed in the forward as well as in the reverse direction and do not go to completion
Proceed in one direction only and go to completion
Stop completely as soon as equilibrium is reached
Proceed only in the reverse direction and do not go to completion
mcqs.why: The chapter defines reversible reactions as those which proceed in the forward as well as in the reverse direction and do not go to completion, unlike irreversible reactions which go to completion in one direction only.

mcqs.q: At dynamic equilibrium, in a closed vessel:
options: The forward reaction stops and only the reverse reaction continues
The concentrations of reactants and products both become zero
The rate of the forward reaction becomes equal to the rate of the reverse reaction
The reverse reaction stops and only the forward reaction continues
mcqs.why: Dynamic equilibrium is the state at which the rate of the forward reaction becomes equal to the rate of the reverse reaction, so the concentrations of reactants and products become constant.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Kc is specific for a reaction, remains constant at a particular temperature, and is independent of pressure, concentration and catalyst.
  • Direction of reaction: if [products]/[reactants] is less than Kc the reaction goes forward, if greater the reverse reaction occurs, and if equal the reaction is at equilibrium.
  • A very large Kc means the reaction is almost complete; a very small Kc means the reaction does not proceed appreciably in the forward direction.
  • Equilibrium needs a closed vessel at constant temperature; in an open vessel gaseous reactants and products escape into the atmosphere.
  • A catalyst cannot change the equilibrium point; it speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions so equilibrium is reached sooner.
  • At equilibrium k1[A][B] = k2[C][D], giving Kc = k1/k2 = [C][D]/[A][B].
  • For 2NO <=> N2 + O2, Kc has no units because the moles of reactants and products are equal.

Solved Exercises

Exercise 3 — Write long answers to the following questions

Q: i. What is the importance of equilibrium constant?

Ans: The value of the equilibrium constant is specific for a reaction and remains constant at a particular temperature. Kc is independent of pressure, concentration and catalyst. Its importance is that it helps us to predict:
(i) Direction of reaction: The direction of a chemical reaction at any particular time can be predicted by means of the [products]/[reactants] ratio. If the ratio is less than Kc, more product is required to attain equilibrium, so the reaction proceeds in the forward direction. If the ratio is greater than Kc, the reverse reaction occurs to attain equilibrium. If the ratio is equal to Kc, the reaction is at equilibrium.
(ii) Extent of reaction: If the equilibrium constant is very large, this indicates that the reaction is almost complete. If the value of Kc is very small, it reflects that the reaction does not proceed appreciably in the forward direction. If the value of Kc is moderate, this shows a very little forward reaction.
(iii) Effect of external conditions: When external conditions such as pressure, temperature and concentration are changed, the position of equilibrium is altered, and the system always tends to restore equilibrium; the value of Kc guides this prediction.

Q: ii. Write down the conditions necessary for equilibrium.

Ans: The following are the conditions of chemical equilibrium:
(i) When a chemical equilibrium is established in a closed vessel at constant temperature, the concentrations of the various species in the reaction become constant. These concentrations are called equilibrium concentrations.
(ii) Equilibrium cannot be attained in an open vessel. In an open vessel the gaseous reactants and products may escape into the atmosphere, leaving behind no possibility of attaining equilibrium.
(iii) A catalyst cannot change the equilibrium point; it only speeds up the rate of both the forward and the reverse reaction, so equilibrium is reached sooner.

Q: iii. What is equilibrium constant? Explain its units.

Ans: For a general reaction A + B <=> C + D, the law of mass action gives: rate of forward reaction r1 = k1[A][B], and rate of reverse reaction r2 = k2[C][D]. At equilibrium the rate of forward reaction is equal to the rate of reverse reaction, so k1[A][B] = k2[C][D], which gives k1/k2 = [C][D]/[A][B]. This ratio k1/k2 is a constant, called the equilibrium constant Kc. Thus Kc may be defined as the ratio of the product of the active masses of the products to the product of the active masses of the reactants. A large value of Kc shows that at equilibrium the product concentrations are greater than those of the reactants, and vice versa.
Units of Kc: The equilibrium constant is a ratio of the product of the concentrations of the products to the product of the concentrations of the reactants, so the unit of Kc depends on the equilibrium constant expression for the given reaction. If the number of moles of reactants and products are equal, the equilibrium constant has no units, as the concentration units cancel out, e.g. for 2NO(g) <=> N2(g) + O2(g), Kc = [N2][O2]/[NO]^2 has no units. If the moles are not equal, Kc has units, e.g. for PCl5 <=> PCl3 + Cl2 the unit of Kc is mol/dm^3.

mcqs.q: The value of the equilibrium constant Kc remains constant:
options: Only when the pressure is changed
Only when a catalyst is added
mcqs.why: The chapter states that the value of the equilibrium constant is specific for a reaction and remains constant at a particular temperature.

mcqs.q: The equilibrium constant Kc is independent of:
mcqs.why: The chapter states that Kc is independent of pressure, concentration and catalyst; it changes only with temperature, remaining constant at a particular temperature.

mcqs.q: If the [products]/[reactants] ratio at any time is less than Kc, then to attain equilibrium:
options: More product is required, so the reaction proceeds in the forward direction
The reverse reaction occurs to attain equilibrium
The reaction is already at equilibrium and nothing changes
More reactant is required, so the reaction proceeds in the reverse direction
mcqs.why: The chapter states that if the ratio is less than Kc, more product is required to attain equilibrium, so the reaction proceeds in the forward direction.

mcqs.q: If the [products]/[reactants] ratio at any time is greater than Kc, then:
options: The reaction proceeds further in the forward direction
The reaction is already at equilibrium and nothing changes
The reverse reaction occurs to attain equilibrium
The value of Kc increases until it equals the ratio
mcqs.why: The chapter states that if the ratio is greater than Kc, the reverse reaction occurs to attain equilibrium.

mcqs.q: If the [products]/[reactants] ratio is equal to Kc, then:
options: The reaction proceeds in the forward direction
The reverse reaction occurs to attain equilibrium
The reaction stops permanently in both directions
mcqs.why: The chapter states that if the ratio is equal to Kc, the reaction is at equilibrium, with the forward and reverse reactions continuing at equal rates.

mcqs.q: If the equilibrium constant is very large, this indicates that:
options: The reaction does not proceed appreciably in the forward direction
Only a very little forward reaction takes place
The reaction cannot attain equilibrium in a closed vessel
mcqs.why: The chapter states that if the equilibrium constant is very large, this indicates that the reaction is almost complete, with product concentrations greater than reactant concentrations.

mcqs.q: Equilibrium cannot be attained in an open vessel because:
options: The temperature in an open vessel cannot be kept constant
A catalyst cannot work in an open vessel
The concentrations in an open vessel keep increasing
The gaseous reactants and products may escape into the atmosphere
mcqs.why: The chapter states that in an open vessel the gaseous reactants and products may escape into the atmosphere, leaving behind no possibility of attaining equilibrium.

mcqs.q: A catalyst affects a system at equilibrium by:
options: Changing the equilibrium point towards the products
Speeding up both the forward and the reverse reaction so equilibrium is reached sooner, without changing the equilibrium point
Changing the equilibrium point towards the reactants
Increasing the value of the equilibrium constant Kc
mcqs.why: The chapter states that a catalyst cannot change the equilibrium point; it only speeds up the rate of both the forward and the reverse reaction, so equilibrium is reached sooner.

mcqs.q: For A + B <=> C + D, applying the law of mass action at equilibrium gives:
mcqs.why: At equilibrium k1[A][B] = k2[C][D], so rearranging gives k1/k2 = [C][D]/[A][B], and this constant ratio k1/k2 is the equilibrium constant Kc.

mcqs.q: For the reaction 2NO(g) <=> N2(g) + O2(g), Kc has no units because:
options: Nitrogen and oxygen are gases while NO is also a gas
The reaction is carried out at constant temperature
The number of moles of reactants and products are equal, so the concentration units cancel out
The equilibrium constant is always without units
mcqs.why: Kc = [N2][O2]/[NO]^2 has two concentration units above and two below, and the chapter states that when the moles of reactants and products are equal the units cancel out.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • According to Bronsted, acids are proton donors and bases are proton accepters.
  • NH3 is a base because it accepts a proton, as in HCl + NH3 -> NH4+ + Cl-.
  • A neutral solution has pH 7; acidic solutions are below 7 and basic solutions are above 7.
  • The lower the pH value, the stronger the acid; strong acids have pH 0 to 3.
  • Bases which give hydroxyl ion in water are called alkalies.
  • KHSO4 is an acidic salt, formed by partial replacement of the hydrogen ions of H2SO4.
  • Sorensen proposed the pH scale in 1909, and pH = -log[H+].
  • A salt consists of the positive ion from the base and the negative ion from the acid.

Solved Exercises

Exercise Q.1 — Select the suitable option

Q: i. According to Bronsted, Acids are:

Options: (a) Proton donor (b) Proton accepter (c) Electron donor (d) Electron accepter

Correct answer: Proton donor

Q: ii. NH3 is ______.

Options: (a) Acid (b) Base (c) Salt (d) Buffer Solution

Correct answer: Base

Q: iii. Neutral solution has a pH value:

Options: (a) 3 (b) 5 (c) 7 (d) 14

Correct answer: 7

Q: iv. Lower the pH value ______ will be an acid.

Options: (a) Weaker (b) Stronger (c) Neutral (d) Alkaline

Correct answer: Stronger

Q: v. Salts are ______ compounds.

Options: (a) Acidic (b) Basic (c) Neutral (d) Neutral

Correct answer: Neutral

Q: vi. Those bases which give hydroxyl ion in water are called.

Options: (a) Acids (b) Alkalies (c) Salts (d) Neutral substances

Correct answer: Alkalies

Q: vii. KHSO4 is a ______ salt.

Options: (a) Basic (b) Acidic (c) Neutral (d) Neutral

Correct answer: Acidic

mcqs.q: i. According to Bronsted, Acids are:
mcqs.why: According to the Bronsted and Lowry concept in the chapter, acids are substances which donate or tend to donate a proton (H+ ion), so an acid is a proton donor.

mcqs.q: ii. NH3 is ______.
mcqs.why: In the chapter example HCl(aq) + NH3(aq) -> NH4+(aq) + Cl-(aq), NH3 accepts a proton and serves as a base, so NH3 is a base.

mcqs.q: iii. Neutral solution has a pH value:
mcqs.why: The chapter states that for a neutral solution pH is equal to 7 and pOH is equal to 7, while acidic solutions are below 7 and basic solutions are above 7.

mcqs.q: iv. Lower the pH value ______ will be an acid.
mcqs.why: The pH scale in the chapter shows strong acids at pH 0 to 3 and weak acids at 4 to 6, so the lower the pH value, the stronger the acid.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an acidic salt?
mcqs.why: The chapter divides salts into three types: neutral salts such as NaCl, acidic salts and basic salts such as Pb(OH)Cl. KHSO4 (potassium hydrogen sulphate) still has a replaceable hydrogen of the acid, so it is an acidic salt. (The book's own MCQ v, 'Salts are ______ compounds', is defective: it keys 'Neutral', although the chapter itself lists neutral, acidic and basic salts, so that item is not quizzed.)

mcqs.q: vi. Those bases which give hydroxyl ion in water are called.
mcqs.why: Under the Arrhenius concept a base gives hydroxyl ion OH- when dissolved in water, and the chapter keys such bases, which give hydroxyl ion in water, as alkalies.

mcqs.q: vii. KHSO4 is a ______ salt.
mcqs.why: The chapter lists KHSO4 as an acidic salt: it is formed when the hydrogen ions of the polybasic acid H2SO4 are only partially replaced, H2SO4 + KOH -> KHSO4 + H2O.

mcqs.q: The pH scale for measuring the strength of acids and bases was proposed by:
mcqs.why: The chapter states that Sorensen in 1909 proposed a scale for the measurement of the strength of acids and bases called the pH scale.

mcqs.q: pH is defined as:
options: The negative logarithm of the molar hydrogen ion concentration, pH = -log[H+]
The positive logarithm of the molar hydrogen ion concentration, pH = log[H+]
The negative logarithm of the molar hydroxide ion concentration, pH = -log[OH-]
The product of the hydrogen ion and hydroxide ion concentrations
mcqs.why: The chapter defines pH as the negative logarithm of the molar hydrogen ion concentration, pH = -log[H+]; the negative logarithm of [OH-] is pOH, not pH.

mcqs.q: A salt is composed of:
options: The positive ion from the acid and the negative ion from the base
The hydrogen ion from the acid and the hydroxyl ion from the base
The positive ion from the base and the negative ion from the acid
Two positive ions, one from the acid and one from the base
mcqs.why: The chapter states that a salt consists of the positive ion from the base and the negative ion from the acid, as NaCl is composed of Na+ from the base and Cl- from the acid.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A double salt is formed by the combination of two simple salts in a fixed proportion which crystallise together, e.g. potash alum K2SO4.Al2(SO4)3.24H2O.
  • Alum is used for water purification to remove suspended impurities by flocculation.
  • Amphoteric substances act both as an acid and as a base; water acts as a base with HCl and as an acid with NH3.
  • A bond pair is shared between two atoms and forms the covalent bond; a lone pair is not shared with any other atom.
  • Compounds with a lone pair can donate it and behave as Lewis bases, e.g. NH3 donates its lone pair to BF3.
  • For 0.001M NaOH, [OH-] = 10^-3, so pOH = 3 and pH = 11.
  • For 0.05M HCl, [H+] = 5 x 10^-2, so pH = 1.30 and pOH = 12.70.

Solved Exercises

Exercise Q.2 — Write short answers to the following questions

Q: i. What are double salts?

Ans: A double salt is a salt formed by the combination of two simple salts in a fixed proportion, which crystallise together as one compound but give the ions of both the salts when dissolved in water. The chapter gives the example of alum or potash alum, K2SO4.Al2(SO4)3.24H2O, which is the double salt of potassium sulphate and aluminium sulphate. It is used for water purification, to remove suspended impurities from water by a process called flocculation.

Q: ii. What are amphoteric substances?

Ans: Those substances which can act both as an acid and as a base are called amphoteric substances, e.g. water. When water is treated with an acid it acts as a base: HCl + H2O -> Cl- + H3O+. When water is treated with a base, it acts as an acid: NH3 + H2O -> NH4+ + OH-.

Q: iii. Differentiate between lone pair and bond pair of electrons.

Ans: A bond pair is the pair of electrons which is shared between two atoms and forms the covalent bond between them. A lone pair is a pair of electrons in the valence shell of an atom which is not shared with any other atom. Compounds having a lone pair of electrons in the valence shell can donate the electron pair and behave as Lewis bases, e.g. NH3 donates its lone pair to form a coordinate covalent bond with BF3.

Q: iv. What will be the pH and pOH of 0.001M NaOH solution?

Ans: NaOH is a strong base and dissociates completely in water.
Step 1: Write the dissociation equation.
NaOH -> Na+ + OH-
Step 2: Find the hydroxide ion concentration.
[OH-] = 0.001 mol/dm^3 = 10^-3 mol/dm^3
Step 3: Use the formula pOH = -log[OH-].
pOH = -log(10^-3)
pOH = -(-3) log 10 = 3
Step 4: Use the relation pH + pOH = 14.
pH = 14 - pOH
pH = 14 - 3 = 11
Final answer: pOH = 3 and pH = 11.

Q: v. Calculate the pH and pOH of 0.05M HCl solution?

Ans: HCl is a strong acid and dissociates completely in water.
Step 1: Write the dissociation equation.
HCl -> H+ + Cl-
Step 2: Find the hydrogen ion concentration.
[H+] = 0.05 mol/dm^3 = 5 x 10^-2 mol/dm^3
Step 3: Use the formula pH = -log[H+].
pH = -log(5 x 10^-2)
pH = -(log 5 + log 10^-2)
pH = -(0.699 - 2) = 1.301, i.e. about 1.30
Step 4: Use the relation pH + pOH = 14.
pOH = 14 - pH
pOH = 14 - 1.30 = 12.70
Final answer: pH = 1.30 and pOH = 12.70.

mcqs.q: A double salt is a salt formed by:
options: The partial replacement of hydrogen ions of an acid by metal ions
The combination of two simple salts in a fixed proportion, which crystallise together as one compound
The partial neutralization of the OH- ions of a base by an acid
The complete replacement of hydrogen ions of an acid by metal ions
mcqs.why: The chapter defines a double salt as a salt formed by the combination of two simple salts in a fixed proportion, which crystallise together but give the ions of both salts when dissolved in water.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A salt is formed by the neutralization reaction of an acid and a base and consists of the positive ion from the base and the negative ion from the acid.
  • Neutral salts form on complete replacement of acid hydrogen ions, e.g. NaCl; acidic salts on partial replacement, e.g. KHSO4 and NaHCO3; basic salts on partial neutralization of base OH- ions, e.g. Pb(OH)Cl.
  • Sorensen proposed the pH scale in 1909; pH = -log[H+] and pOH = -log[OH-], and the scale ranges from 0 to 14.
  • In water Kw = [H+][OH-] = 1 x 10^-14 at 25 degrees C, which gives pH + pOH = 14.
  • Strong acids have pH 0 to 3, weak acids 4 to 6, neutral is 7, weak bases 8 to 11 and strong bases 12 to 14; each whole pH step means ten times more acidic or alkaline.
  • The common ion effect decreases the solubility of an electrolyte when another electrolyte with a common ion is added, suppressing the ionization of the weaker electrolyte.
  • Arrhenius acids give H+ and bases give OH- in water; Bronsted acids donate and bases accept protons; Lewis acids accept and bases donate an electron pair.

Solved Exercises

Exercise Q.3 — Write long answers to the following questions

Q: i. What are salts and explain their different types.

Ans: A compound formed due to the neutralization reaction of an acid and a base is called a salt. A salt consists of the positive ion from the base and the negative ion from the acid. For example, sodium chloride (NaCl) is composed of the sodium (metal) positive ion Na+ and the chloride (non-metal) ion Cl-. Generally salts are ionic compounds. Salts are of three types:
(i) Neutral salts: The salts formed when the hydrogen ions of an acid are completely replaced by metal ions or a group of atoms behaving like metal ions are called neutral (normal) salts. Sodium chloride is formed from sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid: HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O. Other examples are potassium sulphate, sodium sulphate, sodium carbonate, ammonium sulphate and sodium phosphate.
(ii) Acidic salts: Salts formed when hydrogen ions of an acid are partially replaced by metal ions or a group of atoms behaving like metal ions are called acidic salts, e.g. KHSO4, NaHCO3 and (NH4)H2PO4. They are formed by polybasic acids only and can further react with bases forming neutral salts: H2SO4 + KOH -> KHSO4 + H2O.
(iii) Basic salts: Salts formed when the OH- ions of a base are partially neutralized by an acid are called basic salts, e.g. Pb(OH)Cl and Cu(OH)Cl: Pb(OH)2 + HCl -> Pb(OH)Cl + H2O. Basic salts are produced by poly-acid bases.

Q: ii. Write a detailed note on pH.

Ans: Sorensen in 1909 proposed a scale for the measurement of the strength of acids and bases called the pH scale. Here P stands for 'potenz' (the potential to be) and H+ stands for hydrogen ion. pH is the negative logarithm of the molar hydrogen ion concentration: pH = -log[H+]. Similarly, pOH = -log[OH-]. The pH scale measures how acidic or basic a solution is and it ranges from 0 to 14.
In water, the product of the hydronium ion concentration and the hydroxide ion concentration is always 1 x 10^-14 at 25°C: Kw = [H+][OH-] = 10^-14. Taking the negative logarithm gives pH + pOH = 14.
For a neutral solution pH is equal to 7 and pOH is equal to 7. The pH of an acidic solution is less than 7, and the pH of a basic solution is more than 7. Each pH whole number value below 7 is ten times more acidic than the next higher value; for example a pH of 3 is ten times more acidic than a pH of 4 and 100 times more acidic than a pH of 5. The same holds for pH values above 7, each of which is ten times more alkaline than the next lower whole number value. According to the scale given in the chapter, strong acids have pH 0 to 3, weak acids 4 to 6, the value 7 is neutral, weak bases have pH 8 to 11 and strong bases 12 to 14.

Q: iii. Define common ion effect. Explain with example how it effects the chemical reactions.

Ans: The process in which the solubility of an already present electrolyte in solution is decreased by adding another electrolyte having the common ion is called the common ion effect. In this process the solubility of the less soluble electrolyte is decreased by adding a more soluble electrolyte in the solution, where both give a common ion. It affects chemical reactions by suppressing the ionization of the weaker electrolyte, as shown by the following examples from the chapter:
1. When KCl is added into a solution of the less soluble salt KClO3, both give the common K+ ion. Due to the common ion effect the solubility of KClO3 decreases, so KClO3 separates out of the solution as crystals.
2. When HCl is added to a solution of H2S, they produce H+ as the common ion. Because H2S is a weak acid and HCl is a stronger acid, the ionization of H2S is suppressed and thus fewer S2- ions are produced.
3. When NH4Cl is added to a solution of NH4OH, the NH4+ ion is common. Due to the common ion effect the ionization of NH4OH is suppressed and fewer OH- ions are produced.

Q: iv. Write different concepts of acids.

Ans: The different concepts of acids and bases given in the chapter are:
(1) The Arrhenius concept (1884): According to this concept, all those substances which can give H+ ions when dissolved in water are called acids, e.g. HCl(aq) + H2O(l) -> H3O+(aq) + Cl-(aq). A base is a substance which can give hydroxyl ion OH- when dissolved in water, e.g. NaOH(s) -> Na+(aq) + OH-(aq).
(2) Bronsted and Lowry concept: According to this concept, all those substances which donate or tend to donate a proton (H+ ion) are called acids, whereas those substances which accept or tend to accept a proton are known as bases. For example, in HCl(aq) + NH3(aq) -> NH4+(aq) + Cl-(aq), HCl donates a proton and acts as an acid, while NH3 accepts a proton and serves as a base.
(3) The Lewis concept: According to Lewis, those species (molecules or ions) which can accept a pair of electrons are called acids, while those species which can donate a pair of electrons are called bases. An acid-base reaction involves the donation of an electron pair from the base to the acid, forming a coordinate covalent bond.

Q: v. Define Lewis acids and bases, giving examples.

Ans: According to Lewis, those species (molecules or ions) which can accept a pair of electrons are called Lewis acids, while those species which can donate a pair of electrons are called Lewis bases. An acid-base reaction involves the donation of an electron pair from the base to the acid, forming a coordinate covalent bond.
Compounds having less than eight electrons in the valence shell of the central atom, and positive ions, act as Lewis acids. For example, BF3 is a Lewis acid and H+ is a Lewis acid. Compounds having a lone pair of electrons in the valence shell, or negatively charged ions, can donate the electron pair and behave as Lewis bases, e.g. NH3 and H2O.
Examples: NH3 (base) donates its lone pair to BF3 (acid) and forms the complex H3N -> BF3. H+ (acid) accepts the lone pair of NH3 (base) to form the ammonium ion NH4+, and accepts the lone pair of H2O (base) to form the hydronium ion H3O+.

mcqs.why: The chapter states that in water [H+][OH-] = 1 x 10^-14 at 25°C, and taking the negative logarithm of this relation gives pH + pOH = 14.

mcqs.why: The chapter scale gives strong acids pH 0 to 3, weak acids 4 to 6, neutral 7, weak bases 8 to 11 and strong bases 12 to 14.

mcqs.why: Each pH whole number below 7 is ten times more acidic than the next higher value. From pH 5 to pH 3 is two steps, so 10 x 10 = 100 times more acidic.

options: The solubility of an electrolyte is increased by adding another electrolyte having a common ion
The ionization of a strong electrolyte is increased by adding a weak electrolyte

options: HCl and H2S produce S2- as the common ion, and HCl is a weaker acid than H2S

mcqs.why: The chapter explains that HCl and H2S give the common ion H+; because H2S is a weak acid and HCl is a stronger acid, the ionization of H2S is suppressed and fewer S2- ions are produced.

options: Can give hydroxyl ion OH- when dissolved in water

mcqs.why: The chapter states that according to Arrhenius, a base is a substance which can give hydroxyl ion OH- when dissolved in water, e.g. NaOH(s) -> Na+(aq) + OH-(aq).

Key Points

  • Carbon is the essential constituent of all organic compounds.
  • Oxides of carbon, carbonates and bicarbonates are classed as inorganic, not organic.

mcqs.q: i. Which of the following is organic compound.
mcqs.why: Carbon is the essential constituent of organic compounds, but oxides of carbon, carbonates and bicarbonates are excluded and treated as inorganic. CO, CO2 and NaHCO3 fall in those excluded classes, while C2H2 is a hydrocarbon of carbon and hydrogen, so it is organic.

mcqs.q: ii. Which one of the following is the general formula of alkanes.
mcqs.why: The chapter gives the general formula of the alkane homologous series as CnH2n+2, satisfied by methane CH4 (n=1) up to decane C10H22 (n=10). The other formulas do not produce these known members of the series.

mcqs.q: iii. The homologues have the same:
mcqs.why: All members of a homologous series possess the same functional group, so their chemical properties remain the same, while physical properties such as state, colour and density change gradually along the series.

mcqs.q: iv. Carbon atom usually:
mcqs.why: Carbon has four valence electrons and completes its octet by sharing electrons with other atoms, so a carbon atom usually forms four covalent bonds rather than gaining four electrons, losing four electrons or ionizing.

mcqs.q: v. Organic radical with general formula CnH2n+1 is:
mcqs.why: Radicals derived from alkanes by the removal of one H-atom are alkyl groups with the general formula CnH2n+1, as derived in the chapter for methyl, ethyl, propyl, butyl and pentyl, so the radical is an alkyl group.

mcqs.q: vi. The next homologue of C8H18 is:
mcqs.why: Adjacent homologues differ by one CH2 unit. Adding CH2 to octane C8H18 gives carbon 8+1 = 9 and hydrogen 18+2 = 20, that is C9H20, which the chapter lists as nonane, the next homologue after octane.

mcqs.q: vii. Methane is the first member of:
mcqs.why: The chapter lists the alkane homologous series beginning with methane CH4 as its first member, followed by ethane, propane and butane, all fitting the general formula CnH2n+2.

mcqs.q: viii. The compound C3H8 must have:
mcqs.why: C3H8 is propane, an alkane fitting CnH2n+2 with n=3, giving H = 2(3)+2 = 8. Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons, so every bond in propane is a single covalent bond.

mcqs.q: ix. Organic compounds are originated from.
mcqs.why: Organic compounds were originally obtained from vegetables and animals, that is from living organisms, which is why the branch is called organic chemistry; air, rock and sun are sources of inorganic materials instead.

mcqs.q: x. The name of C6H14 is:
mcqs.why: The chapter's alkane list names the six-carbon member hexane, C6H14, which also fits CnH2n+2 with n=6, giving H = 2(6)+2 = 14. Propane, heptane and decane have 3, 7 and 10 carbons respectively.

mcqs.why: CH3OH, C2H5OH and C5H11OH all carry the -OH functional group of the alcohols, so they share similar chemical properties. C2H5COOH carries the carboxylic acid functional group instead, so its chemical properties are different.

mcqs.q: xii. Which of the following is inorganic:
mcqs.why: CH4, CH3OH and CH3Cl are covalent carbon compounds and are organic. NaCN is a metal cyanide salt, classed with the inorganic compounds, just as carbonates and metal carbides are excluded from organic compounds.

mcqs.q: In Wohler's synthesis, urea was obtained by heating which inorganic substance?
mcqs.why: The chapter shows NH4Cl heated with KCNO first giving ammonium cyanate NH4CNO, and heating ammonium cyanate then gives urea NH2CONH2, so ammonium cyanate is the inorganic substance directly converted into urea.

mcqs.q: Adjacent members of a homologous series differ from each other by:
mcqs.why: By definition a homologous series is a series of compounds in which adjacent members differ by a CH2 unit, and the short answers repeat that each member differs from its adjacent member by one CH2 (methylene) group only.

mcqs.q: The alkyl group obtained by removing one hydrogen atom from ethane is:
mcqs.why: Alkyl names are formed by replacing -ane with -yl. Ethane C2H6 minus one H-atom gives -C2H5, named ethyl, just as methane gives methyl -CH3 and propane gives propyl -C3H7.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Organic compounds are covalent with low boiling points, so they evaporate easily and are volatile.
  • Most organic compounds are non-polar, soluble in acetone, ether and benzene but insoluble in polar water.
  • A functional group replaces a hydrogen atom of an alkane and gives the molecule its characteristic chemical properties.
  • A functional group is not a molecule by itself; in methanol CH3OH, -CH3 is R and -OH is the functional group.
  • Wohler synthesized urea from ammonium cyanate in 1828, which discarded the vital force theory.
  • Hydrocarbons burn in air to give carbon dioxide, water and heat energy.
  • Homologues share the same functional group and differ by one CH2 group, so their chemical properties are the same.

Solved Exercises

Exercise Q.2 — Write answers for the given questions

Q: i. Why organic compounds are volatile in nature?

Ans: Organic compounds are generally covalent in nature and have low melting and boiling points. Because of their low boiling points they evaporate easily on heating, so they are volatile in nature.

Q: ii. Organic compounds are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents. Why?

Ans: Most of the organic compounds are non-polar in nature, so they are soluble in non-polar solvents such as acetone, ether and benzene etc. They are less soluble or insoluble in water, which is a polar solvent.

Q: iii. Functional group is a group of atoms but not a molecule. Explain.

Ans: A functional group is an atom or group of atoms which replaces the hydrogen atom in an alkane and gives the molecule its characteristic chemical properties. It is not a molecule by itself, because an organic compound is composed of two parts: (i) the hydrocarbon part, which is the alkyl group -R, and (ii) the functional group part. The functional group exists only as a part of a complete molecule; for example, in methanol, CH3OH, -CH3 is R and -OH is the functional group, and -OH alone is not a separate molecule.

Q: iv. Organic substances can be made from inorganic substances. Explain.

Ans: This was proved by Friedrich Wohler, a German chemist, who in 1828 synthesized the organic substance urea in the laboratory from the inorganic substance ammonium cyanate. Ammonium cyanate is obtained by heating solid ammonium chloride with solid potassium cyanate:
NH4Cl(s) + KCNO(s) --heat--> NH4CNO(s) + KCl(s)
NH4CNO(s) --heat--> NH2CONH2(s) (Urea)
Thus an organic substance (urea) was made from inorganic substances, without any living organism.

Q: v. Why the vital force theory was discarded?

Ans: It was assumed that organic compounds could only be produced by living organisms under the influence of a supernatural force called the Vital Force. In 1828 Friedrich Wohler synthesized the organic substance urea in the laboratory from the inorganic substance ammonium cyanate. This synthesis proved that the formation of an organic compound is no more dependent on the vital force and that the influence of a living organism is not necessary for the production of organic compounds, so the vital force theory was discarded.

Q: vi. Why are hydrocarbons combustible?

Ans: Most of the organic compounds are inflammable and burn in air to give carbon dioxide, water and heat energy. Hydrocarbons are made up of only carbon and hydrogen, and both of these burn in air, so hydrocarbons are combustible. Thus most fuels such as natural gas, petrol and coal are organic, and their combustion or burning is our main source of heat energy.

Q: vii. The chemical properties of a homologous series are always the same. Explain.

Ans: Yes. Organic compounds are classified into various groups or series on the basis that all the members in a particular series possess the same functional group and have the same chemical properties. Each member of the series differs from its adjacent member by one CH2 (methylene) group only, so the chemical properties of all the homologues remain the same, e.g. all the alkanes have similar chemical properties.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A homologous series has adjacent members differing by CH2, with the same functional group, chemical properties and general formula.
  • There are seven homologous series, including hydrocarbons, alcohols, carboxylic acids, carbonyl compounds, alkyl halides, amines and ethers.
  • Alkanes up to ten carbons run from methane CH4 to decane C10H22 following CnH2n+2.
  • Alkyl groups form by removing one H-atom from an alkane and replacing -ane by -yl, e.g. methyl -CH3 and pentyl -C5H11.
  • Organic compounds have low melting and boiling points, are inflammable and covalent, and are poor conductors of electricity.
  • Organic reactions are much slower than inorganic reactions and many organic compounds are thermally unstable.
  • Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds except oxides of carbon, carbonates, bicarbonates and some metal carbides.

Solved Exercises

Exercise Q.3 — Write long answers of the given questions

Q: i. What is a homologous series? Give the names of alkane homologous series up to ten C-atoms.

Ans: A homologous series may be defined as a series of compounds in which adjacent members differ by a CH2 unit. All the members in a particular series possess the same functional group and have the same chemical properties and the same general formula. The individual member of the series is called a homologue. There are seven homologous series of organic compounds: hydrocarbons, alcohols, carboxylic acids, carbonyl compounds, alkyl halides, amines and ethers.
The alkane homologous series (general formula CnH2n+2) up to ten carbon atoms is:
1 C-atom: Methane, CH4
2 C-atoms: Ethane, C2H6
3 C-atoms: Propane, C3H8
4 C-atoms: Butane, C4H10
5 C-atoms: Pentane, C5H12
6 C-atoms: Hexane, C6H14
7 C-atoms: Heptane, C7H16
8 C-atoms: Octane, C8H18
9 C-atoms: Nonane, C9H20
10 C-atoms: Decane, C10H22

Q: ii. What are alkyl groups? Name and derive the alkyl groups from the first five members of alkane series.

Ans: The radicals or groups derived from alkanes by the removal of one H-atom are called alkyl radicals or alkyl groups. They are denoted by the general symbol -R. The formula of an alkyl group is CnH2n+1, where n is the number of carbon atoms = 1, 2, 3... The name of an alkyl group is derived from the name of the corresponding alkane by replacing the -ane by -yl.
The alkyl groups from the first five members of the alkane series are:
Methane, CH4 — removing one H-atom gives Methyl, -CH3
Ethane, C2H6 — removing one H-atom gives Ethyl, -C2H5
Propane, C3H8 — removing one H-atom gives Propyl, -C3H7
Butane, C4H10 — removing one H-atom gives Butyl, -C4H9
Pentane, C5H12 — removing one H-atom gives Pentyl, -C5H11

Q: iii. Give characteristic properties of organic compounds. Why organic compounds are placed in a separate branch of chemistry?

Ans: Organic compounds have many common characteristics which are entirely different from inorganic compounds. Some of their general characteristics are:
1. Composition: Carbon is the essential constituent of all organic compounds.
2. Low melting and boiling points: Organic compounds have generally low melting and boiling points and are volatile in nature.
3. Thermal instability: Many organic compounds are thermally unstable and generally decompose at high temperature into simple substances.
4. Inflammability: Most of the organic compounds are inflammable and burn in air to give carbon dioxide, water and heat energy.
5. Bonding: Organic compounds are generally covalent in nature.
6. Solubility: Most organic compounds are non-polar, so they are soluble in non-polar solvents such as acetone, ether and benzene, and are less or insoluble in water, which is polar.
7. Electrical conductivity: Because of the non-polar covalent bonds present in most organic compounds, they are poor conductors of electricity both in the fused state and in solution form.
8. Reactivity: Reactions involving organic compounds are much slower than the reactions which involve inorganic substances.
Organic compounds are placed in a separate branch of chemistry because they have common features entirely different from inorganic compounds and they exist in a very large number — there are millions of organic compounds and several thousand new compounds are synthesized each year.

Q: iv. What is organic chemistry? Briefly discuss how organic and inorganic compound differ.

Ans: The branch of chemistry which deals with the study of organic compounds is called organic chemistry. Organic compounds are the compounds of carbon (except the oxides of carbon, carbonates, bicarbonates and some metal carbides); they essentially contain carbon and hydrogen and occasionally a few other elements such as oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur, phosphorus and halogens.
Organic and inorganic compounds differ as follows: (1) Source: inorganic compounds were derived from the earth crust, while organic compounds were obtained from vegetables and animals, i.e. from living organisms, e.g. table salt (NaCl), marble (CaCO3) and carbon dioxide (CO2) are inorganic, whereas urea (from urine), tartaric acid (from grapes), citric acid (from lemons) and sucrose (from cane sugar) are organic. (2) Composition: carbon is the essential constituent of organic compounds, while inorganic compounds may contain any elements. (3) Bonding: organic compounds are generally covalent in nature, while inorganic compounds are generally ionic. (4) Melting and boiling points: organic compounds have low melting and boiling points and are volatile, while inorganic compounds have high melting and boiling points. (5) Solubility: organic compounds are mostly non-polar and are soluble in non-polar solvents but insoluble in water, while inorganic compounds are mostly soluble in water. (6) Conductivity: organic compounds are poor conductors of electricity, while inorganic compounds conduct electricity in the fused state or in solution. (7) Reactivity: reactions of organic compounds are much slower than those of inorganic substances.

lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Dehydration of ethyl alcohol with conc. H2SO4 forms ethene.
  • Ethene adds HBr to form bromoethane, CH3-CH2-Br.
  • Acetylene adds 2HBr to form 1,1-dibromoethane, CH3-CHBr2.
  • The general formula of alkenes is CnH2n and of alkanes is CnH2n+2.
  • Baeyer's reagent is alkaline KMnO4 and Baeyer's test shows the presence of a double bond.
  • Acetylene with alkaline KMnO4 gives a carboxylic acid and CO2.
  • Ethane is the least reactive hydrocarbon and reacts with chlorine in the presence of sunlight.
  • Unsaturated hydrocarbons decolourise bromine water by addition across the multiple bond.

Solved Exercises

Exercise Q.1 — Choose the correct option from the given choices

Q: i. Dehydration of ethyl alcohol with conc. H2SO4 results in the formation of:

Options: (a) Ethane (b) Methane (c) Acetylene (d) Ethene

Q: ii. Which one of the following reagents distinguishes ethene from acetylene:

Options: (a) Alkaline solution of KMnO4 (b) Bromine solution (c) Carbon tetrachloride solution (d) Alcoholic KOH

Correct answer: Alcoholic KOH

Q: iii. The final product X in the following reaction is: HC≡CH + 2HBr -> X

Options: (a) BrCH = CHBr (1,2-dibromoethene) (b) CH3-CHBr2 (1,1-dibromoethane) (c) CHBr2-CHBr2 (1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane) (d) CHBr3

Correct answer: CH3-CHBr2 (1,1-dibromoethane)

Q: iv. Which one of the following decolourises Br2 water:

Options: (a) Propane (b) Ethene (c) Ethane (d) Methane

Correct answer: Ethene

Q: v. Ethene reacts with HBr, the compound formed is:

Options: (a) CH3-CH2-Br (b) Br-CH2-CH2-Br (c) CH3-CH2-CH3 (d) Acetylene

Correct answer: CH3-CH2-Br

Q: vi. Which of the following statements is not true for alkynes:

Options: (a) They contain a triple bond (b) They burn to form CO2 (c) They perform Baeyer's test (d) They undergo addition reaction

Correct answer: They perform Baeyer's test

Q: vii. General formula for alkenes is:

Options: (a) CnH2nOn (b) CnH2n-1 (c) CnH2n-2 (d) CnH2n

Correct answer: CnH2n

Q: viii. All the members of alkane series have:

Options: (a) All single bonds (b) At least one double bond (c) At least one triple bond (d) All types of bonds

Correct answer: All single bonds

Q: ix. Baeyer's reagent is:

Options: (a) Conc. KMnO4 (b) Alkaline KMnO4 (c) Acidic KMnO4 (d) Hot KMnO4

Correct answer: Alkaline KMnO4

Q: x. Which one gives carboxylic acid with alkaline KMnO4:

Options: (a) Ethane (b) Ethene (c) Acetylene (d) Methane

Correct answer: Acetylene

Q: xi. Which one gives a mixture of hydrocarbons on halogenation:

Options: (a) Ethyne (b) Ethene (c) Ethane (d) Ethyl alcohol

Correct answer: Ethane

Q: xii. Baeyer's test shows the presence of:

Options: (a) A single bond (b) A double bond (c) A triple bond (d) No bond

Correct answer: A double bond

Q: xiii. Which one is the least reactive:

Options: (a) Ethyne (b) Propene (c) Ethene (d) Ethane

Correct answer: Ethane

Options: (a) Carbon tetra chloride (b) Ether (c) Sunlight (d) water

Correct answer: Sunlight

mcqs.q: i. Dehydration of ethyl alcohol with conc. H2SO4 results in the formation of:
mcqs.why: Dehydration means removal of water. Ethyl alcohol loses a water molecule when heated with concentrated H2SO4 and forms ethene, CH2=CH2, the alkene containing a double bond; ethane, methane and acetylene are not formed in this reaction.

mcqs.q: Acetylene (ethyne) is prepared by reacting 1,2-dibromoethane with:
mcqs.why: The chapter's preparation of alkynes states that 1,2-dihalides react with alcoholic potassium hydroxide and two molecules of hydrogen halide are eliminated: 1,2-dibromoethane first forms bromoethene and then acetylene. Zinc dust is used for dehalogenation of tetrahalides instead. (The book's own MCQ ii keys alcoholic KOH as a reagent distinguishing ethene from acetylene, but no such test appears in the chapter — both gases decolourise KMnO4 and bromine water — so that item is not quizzed.)

mcqs.q: iii. The final product X in the following reaction is: HC≡CH + 2HBr -> X
mcqs.why: The chapter gives the addition of hydrogen bromide to ethyne as HC≡CH + 2HBr -> CH3-CHBr2, where both bromine atoms add to the same carbon atom, giving 1,1-dibromoethane as the final product X.

mcqs.q: iv. Which one of the following decolourises Br2 water:
mcqs.why: Ethene contains a double bond and adds bromine across it, CH2=CH2 + Br2 -> CH2Br-CH2Br, so the red colour of bromine water disappears. Propane, ethane and methane are saturated alkanes and do not decolourise bromine water.

mcqs.q: v. Ethene reacts with HBr, the compound formed is:
mcqs.why: The chapter gives the addition of hydrogen halides to alkenes as CH2=CH2 + HBr -> CH3-CH2-Br, so ethene reacts with HBr to form bromoethane, with H and Br adding across the double bond.

mcqs.q: Which of the following statements is not true for alkynes:
mcqs.why: Alkynes are unsaturated hydrocarbons: they contain a triple bond, burn to form CO2 and undergo addition reactions. They also perform Baeyer's test — the chapter states ethyne is oxidised by alkaline KMnO4, discharging its purple colour. (The book's own version of this MCQ keys 'They perform Baeyer's test' as the untrue statement, which contradicts the chapter's own oxidation answers, so the item is corrected here.)

mcqs.q: vii. General formula for alkenes is:
mcqs.why: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing at least one double bond between two carbon atoms, and their general molecular formula is CnH2n, with two hydrogen atoms less than the corresponding alkanes CnH2n+2.

mcqs.q: viii. All the members of alkane series have:
mcqs.why: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons in which each carbon atom is linked by single covalent bonds only and uses all its four valence electrons; double bonds belong to alkenes and triple bonds to alkynes, not to the alkane series.

mcqs.q: ix. Baeyer's reagent is:
mcqs.why: Baeyer's reagent is alkaline potassium permanganate. Alkenes react with cold dilute alkaline KMnO4 to form glycols and its purple colour disappears, and this reaction is called Baeyer's test.

mcqs.q: x. Which one gives carboxylic acid with alkaline KMnO4:
mcqs.why: The chapter's oxidation of ethyne with alkaline KMnO4 breaks the molecule at the C-C triple bond and gives a carboxylic acid and carbon dioxide: R-C≡C-H + 4[O] --KMnO4--> R-COOH + CO2. Ethene instead gives ethylene glycol.

mcqs.q: xi. Which one gives a mixture of hydrocarbons on halogenation:
mcqs.why: Halogenation of an alkane is a substitution reaction carried out in sunlight, in which hydrogen atoms are replaced one by one, so ethane gives a mixture of halogenated hydrocarbons; ethene and ethyne give single addition products instead.

mcqs.q: xii. Baeyer's test shows the presence of:
mcqs.why: Baeyer's test is described in the chapter as a very useful test for the detection of a double bond: alkenes decolourise cold dilute KMnO4 solution as they are oxidized to glycols and the purple colour disappears.

mcqs.q: xiii. Which one is the least reactive:
mcqs.why: Ethane is a saturated alkane containing only single covalent bonds and is chemically inert, while ethyne, propene and ethene are unsaturated and readily undergo addition reactions, so ethane is the least reactive of the four.

mcqs.q: xiv. Ethane reacts with chlorine in the presence of:
mcqs.why: Alkanes are chemically inert paraffins and give substitution reactions such as halogenation only in the presence of sunlight; the chapter states alkanes react with halogens in sunlight, not in carbon tetrachloride, ether or water.

mcqs.q: Ethane can be produced from ethene by hydrogenation using which catalyst?
mcqs.why: The chapter gives the hydrogenation as CH2=CH2 + H2 --Ni, 200-300°C--> CH3-CH3, so nickel is the catalyst. Zinc dust is used in dehalogenation and reduction, PCl3 in the halogenation of ethyne, and CCl4 is an inert solvent.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Alkanes are saturated and inert because each carbon uses all four valence electrons in single bonds; paraffin means little affinity.
  • Baeyer's test: alkenes react with cold dilute KMnO4 to form glycols and the purple colour disappears.
  • Saturated hydrocarbons contain only single covalent bonds, e.g. methane and ethane, with general formula CnH2n+2.
  • Addition reactions add atoms or groups across a double or triple bond and convert unsaturated compounds into saturated ones.
  • Alkenes contain at least one double bond, have general formula CnH2n and two hydrogen atoms less than the corresponding alkanes.
  • Ethene is hydrogenated to ethane with hydrogen over nickel catalyst at 200-300°C.
  • Alkynes are prepared by dehydrohalogenation of 1,2-dihalides with alcoholic KOH and by dehalogenation of tetrahalides with zinc dust.

Solved Exercises

Exercise Q.2 — Write short answers for the given questions

Q: i. Why alkane is inert in nature?

Ans: Alkanes contain single covalent bonds between C-C and C-H atoms. Each carbon atom of an alkane is linked to four other atoms and uses all its four valence electrons, so alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons. Therefore this class of hydrocarbons is chemically inert. They are sometimes referred to as paraffins, which is a Latin word meaning 'little affinity'.

Q: ii. What is Baeyer's test?

Ans: Alkenes react with cold dilute potassium permanganate solution to form glycols. Potassium permanganate is changed to manganese dioxide and potassium hydroxide, so its purple colour disappears. This is a very useful test for the detection of a double bond and is called Baeyer's test:
3CH2=CH2 + 2KMnO4 + 4H2O -> 3CH2(OH)-CH2(OH) (ethylene glycol) + 2MnO2 + 2KOH

Q: iii. What do you mean by saturated hydrocarbons?

Ans: Saturated hydrocarbons are those hydrocarbons which contain only single covalent bonds between the carbon atoms. Each carbon atom is linked to four other atoms, e.g. the alkanes, which have the general formula CnH2n+2, such as methane (CH4) and ethane (C2H6).

Q: iv. What are addition reactions?

Ans: Addition reactions are the reactions in which atoms or groups are added across a double or triple bond, so that an unsaturated compound is converted into a saturated compound. Because of their unsaturated nature, alkenes and alkynes easily undergo addition reactions. For example, chlorine and bromine readily add to the double bond of alkenes to form dihalo compounds: CH2=CH2 + Br2 --CCl4--> CH2Br-CH2Br (1,2-dibromoethane).

Q: v. What is alkene? Give examples.

Ans: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing at least one double bond between two carbon atoms. The general molecular formula of alkenes is CnH2n, so alkenes have two hydrogen atoms less than the corresponding alkanes. Examples are ethene (CH2=CH2), propene and butene.

Q: vi. Why alkenes are more reactive than the corresponding alkane?

Ans: Alkenes contain a double bond between two carbon atoms, so they are unsaturated. Because of this unsaturated nature they easily undergo addition reactions and are converted into saturated compounds. Alkanes, on the other hand, contain only single covalent bonds and are chemically inert, so alkenes are more reactive than the corresponding alkanes.

Q: vii. How ethane can be produced from ethene?

Ans: Ethane is produced from ethene by hydrogenation. Ethene reacts with hydrogen in the presence of nickel as catalyst at 200-300°C to form ethane:
CH2=CH2 + H2 --Ni, 200-300°C--> CH3-CH3

Q: viii. Why addition reactions take place in ethene and ethyne but not in ethane?

Ans: Ethene contains a double bond and ethyne contains a triple bond, so both are unsaturated hydrocarbons and easily undergo addition reactions, in which the multiple bond breaks and atoms are added to the two carbon atoms. Ethane is a saturated hydrocarbon containing only single covalent bonds; it has no multiple bond to break, so it does not undergo addition reactions and gives substitution reactions instead.

Q: ix. Write down two methods of preparation of alkyne?

Ans: Two methods of preparation of alkynes are:
(1) Dehydrohalogenation of 1,2-dihalides: Alkynes are obtained by reacting 1,2-dihalides with alcoholic potassium hydroxide; two molecules of hydrogen halide are eliminated. Acetylene is prepared from 1,2-dibromoethane in two steps: first bromoethene is formed, then the second molecule of HBr is eliminated and acetylene (ethyne) is obtained.
(2) Dehalogenation of tetrahalides: Tetrahaloalkanes are heated with an active metal like zinc dust to produce alkynes, e.g. 1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane + 2Zn -> HC≡CH (ethyne) + 2ZnBr2.

mcqs.q: Alkanes are called paraffins, a Latin word meaning:
mcqs.why: Each carbon atom of an alkane is linked to four other atoms and uses all its four valence electrons in single bonds, so alkanes are saturated and chemically inert; they are called paraffins, meaning little affinity.

mcqs.q: What is formed when ethene reacts with cold dilute KMnO4 solution in Baeyer's test?
mcqs.why: The chapter's Baeyer's test equation is 3CH2=CH2 + 2KMnO4 + 4H2O -> 3CH2(OH)-CH2(OH) (ethylene glycol) + 2MnO2 + 2KOH, and the purple colour of KMnO4 disappears during the reaction.

mcqs.q: Saturated hydrocarbons contain which type of bonds between the carbon atoms?
mcqs.why: Saturated hydrocarbons are those which contain only single covalent bonds between the carbon atoms, each carbon being linked to four other atoms, e.g. the alkanes methane CH4 and ethane C2H6 with general formula CnH2n+2.

mcqs.q: In an addition reaction, an unsaturated compound is converted into:
mcqs.why: Addition reactions are those in which atoms or groups are added across a double or triple bond, so that an unsaturated compound is converted into a saturated compound, as when Br2 adds to ethene forming 1,2-dibromoethane.

mcqs.q: An alkene has how many hydrogen atoms less than the corresponding alkane?
mcqs.why: The general molecular formula of alkenes is CnH2n while that of alkanes is CnH2n+2, so alkenes have two hydrogen atoms less than the corresponding alkanes because of the double bond.

mcqs.q: Alkenes are more reactive than the corresponding alkanes because they:
options: Contain a double bond and are unsaturated
mcqs.why: Alkenes contain a double bond between two carbon atoms, so they are unsaturated and easily undergo addition reactions, whereas alkanes contain only single covalent bonds and are chemically inert.

mcqs.q: Hydrogenation of ethene to ethane is carried out over nickel catalyst at:
mcqs.why: The solved answer gives the hydrogenation as CH2=CH2 + H2 --Ni, 200-300°C--> CH3-CH3, so ethene is converted into ethane by hydrogen in the presence of nickel as catalyst at 200-300 degrees Celsius.

mcqs.q: Ethane does not undergo addition reactions because it:
options: Has no multiple bond to break
mcqs.why: Ethene has a double bond and ethyne a triple bond, so atoms can add across them, but ethane is a saturated hydrocarbon containing only single covalent bonds with no multiple bond to break, so it gives substitution reactions instead.

mcqs.q: Acetylene is prepared from 1,2-dibromoethane by dehydrohalogenation using:
mcqs.why: Alkynes are obtained by reacting 1,2-dihalides with alcoholic potassium hydroxide; two molecules of HBr are eliminated in two steps from 1,2-dibromoethane, first forming bromoethene and then acetylene.

mcqs.q: In the dehalogenation method, tetrahaloalkanes are heated with which active metal to produce alkynes?
mcqs.why: The chapter gives the dehalogenation as 1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane + 2Zn -> HC≡CH (ethyne) + 2ZnBr2, so tetrahaloalkanes are heated with an active metal like zinc dust to produce alkynes.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Alkanes are saturated and inert and give substitution reactions; alkenes are unsaturated and reactive and give addition reactions.
  • Alkanes are prepared by hydrogenation of alkenes and alkynes over nickel and by reduction of alkyl halides with nascent hydrogen from Zn + HCl.
  • Alkenes add halogens in CCl4 and add HBr to form alkyl halides; their hydrogenation converts vegetable oils into ghee.
  • Ethene is oxidized by cold dilute KMnO4 to ethylene glycol, while ethyne is oxidized by alkaline KMnO4 to a carboxylic acid and CO2.
  • Ethyne halogenation adds two halogen molecules in two steps to give a tetrahalide, using PCl3 as catalyst; iodine reacts slowly.
  • Ethyne hydrogenation needs 2H2 over nickel at 200-300°C to form ethane.
  • The first four alkanes are gases, the next thirteen members are colourless liquids and the higher alkanes are solids.

Solved Exercises

Exercise Q.3 — Write long answers of the following questions

Q: i. Differentiate between alkanes and alkenes. Give methods of preparation for alkanes.

Ans: Differences between alkanes and alkenes:
(1) Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons containing only single covalent bonds, while alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing at least one double bond between two carbon atoms.
(2) The general formula of alkanes is CnH2n+2, while the general formula of alkenes is CnH2n; alkenes have two hydrogen atoms less than the corresponding alkanes.
(3) Alkanes are chemically inert (paraffins, 'little affinity') and give substitution reactions, e.g. halogenation in sunlight. Alkenes are very reactive compounds and readily undergo addition reactions and become saturated.
(4) Alkanes do not decolourise alkaline KMnO4, while alkenes are easily oxidized by cold dilute KMnO4 and decolourise its purple colour (Baeyer's test).
(5) The first four alkanes are gases, the next thirteen members are colourless liquids and the higher alkanes are solids.
Methods of preparation of alkanes:
(1) Hydrogenation of alkenes and alkynes: Unsaturated hydrocarbons like alkenes and alkynes react with hydrogen in the presence of nickel as catalyst at 200-300°C to form alkanes. CH2=CH2 + H2 --Ni, 200-300°C--> CH3-CH3; CH≡CH + 2H2 --Ni, 200-300°C--> CH3-CH3.
(2) Reduction of alkyl halides: Alkyl halides on reduction with nascent hydrogen (from Zn + HCl) form the corresponding alkanes: R-X + 2[H] --Zn + HCl--> RH + HX. For example, methyl iodide gives methane: CH3-I + 2[H] --Zn + HCl--> CH4 + HI.

Q: ii. Give important reactions of alkenes.

Ans: Because of the unsaturated nature of alkenes, they easily undergo addition reactions and in this way are converted into saturated compounds. Their important reactions are:
1. Addition of halogens: Chlorine and bromine readily add to the double bond of alkenes in the presence of an inert solvent like carbon tetrachloride to form dihalo compounds; no high temperature or sunlight is needed. Addition of bromine to ethene decolourises the red colour of bromine and produces 1,2-dibromoethane: CH2=CH2 + Br2 --CCl4--> CH2Br-CH2Br.
2. Addition of hydrogen halides: A molecule of hydrogen halide adds to an alkene giving the corresponding alkyl halide: CH2=CH2 + HBr -> CH3-CH2-Br (bromoethane).
3. Oxidation by KMnO4: Alkenes react with cold dilute potassium permanganate solution to form glycols (alcohols containing two hydroxyl groups on two adjacent carbons). The purple colour of KMnO4 disappears; this is Baeyer's test for the detection of a double bond: 3CH2=CH2 + 2KMnO4 + 4H2O -> 3CH2(OH)-CH2(OH) + 2MnO2 + 2KOH.
4. Hydrogenation: Alkenes readily react with hydrogen in the presence of nickel as catalyst at 240°C forming the corresponding alkanes. Hydrogenation is an exothermic process: CH2=CH2 + H2 --Ni, 240°C--> CH3-CH3 + Heat. Hydrogenation of alkenes is industrially used for the conversion of vegetable oils into ghee.

Q: iii. Give oxidation reactions of ethene and ethyne.

Ans: Oxidation of ethene: Ethene reacts with cold dilute potassium permanganate solution and is oxidized to ethylene glycol, a glycol containing two hydroxyl groups (-OH) on two adjacent carbons. Potassium permanganate is changed to manganese dioxide and potassium hydroxide, so its purple colour disappears (Baeyer's test):
3CH2=CH2 + 2KMnO4 + 4H2O -> 3CH2(OH)-CH2(OH) + 2MnO2 + 2KOH
Oxidation of ethyne: The oxidation of alkynes with alkaline potassium permanganate gives a carboxylic acid and carbon dioxide, the molecule breaking at the C-C triple bond:
R-C≡C-H + 4[O] --KMnO4--> R-COOH + CO2

Q: iv. Give important reactions of ethyne.

Ans: Because of the unsaturated nature of alkynes, they easily undergo addition reactions and in this way are converted into saturated hydrocarbons. The important reactions of ethyne are:
1. Halogenation: Addition of halogen at the triple bond is called halogenation. Two molecules of halogen add to the triple bond in two steps, forming a dihalide and then a tetrahalide. Chlorine and bromine react readily while iodine reacts slowly; PCl3 is used as a catalyst:
HC≡CH + Cl2 --PCl3--> CHCl=CHCl (1,2-dichloroethene)
CHCl=CHCl + Cl2 --PCl3--> CHCl2-CHCl2 (1,1,2,2-tetrachloroethane)
2. Oxidation with KMnO4: The oxidation of alkynes with alkaline potassium permanganate gives a carboxylic acid and carbon dioxide on breaking the molecule at the C-C triple bond: R-C≡C-H + 4[O] --KMnO4--> R-COOH + CO2.
3. Hydrogenation: Ethyne reacts with hydrogen in the presence of nickel as catalyst at 200-300°C to form ethane: CH≡CH + 2H2 --Ni, 200-300°C--> CH3-CH3.
4. Addition of hydrogen bromide: HC≡CH + 2HBr -> CH3-CHBr2 (1,1-dibromoethane).

mcqs.q: In the reduction method, alkyl halides are reduced to alkanes by nascent hydrogen obtained from:

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Main sources of carbohydrates include sugarcane, sugarbeet, honey, wheat, rice, maize and potatoes; all are of plant origin except lactose.
  • Cellulose is the basic component of paper, and cotton carbohydrates are used in the textile industry.
  • Cardiac glycosides are used to normalize heartbeat, and carbohydrate fibres help control constipation and diarrhoea.
  • Proteins contain peptide bondings, hydrogen bondings and disulfide bridges; disulfide bridges occur only in sulphur-containing proteins.
  • Denaturing changes the natural folded structure of a protein on heating or chemical treatment, without breaking its peptide bonds.
  • Fats are solid or semisolid because saturated fatty acids predominate, while oils are liquid because unsaturated fatty acids predominate.
  • Each nucleotide consists of a sugar, a nitrogenous base (purine or pyrimidine) and a phosphate group.

Solved Exercises

Exercise Q.2 — Write short answers to the following questions

Q: i. Describe some of the sources and uses of carbohydrates.

Ans: Sources of carbohydrates: The main sources of carbohydrates are sugarcane, sugarbeet, pineapple, apricot, mango, honey, wheat, rice, maize and potatoes etc. All the carbohydrates are of plant origin except lactose, which is of animal origin.
Uses of carbohydrates: (1) Textile industry: carbohydrates like cotton are used in the manufacturing of cloths. (2) Paper industry: cellulose is the basic component of paper. (3) Medical uses: cardiac glycosides are used to normalize heartbeat; constipation and diarrhoea are mainly controlled by the use of carbohydrate fibres. Carbohydrates also act as a chief source of energy and as structural components in living organisms; their main function is to support plant structure (cellulose) and to store chemical energy in the form of glycogen and starch.

Q: ii. Explain bonding in protein molecules in your own words.

Ans: In protein molecules three types of bondings may occur: (i) peptide bondings, (ii) hydrogen bondings and (iii) disulfide bridges. Protein molecules are formed due to amino acid condensation (with the removal of a water molecule), in which the amino acids are joined together by peptide linkage, giving a linear sequence of a protein polymer. Disulfide bridges are found only in sulphur-containing protein molecules. Due to the presence of hydrogen bonding and sulphide bridges, protein molecules get folded and refolded to give secondary, tertiary and quaternary structures.

Q: iii. What is meant by denaturing of proteins? Explain.

Ans: Denaturing is the change of the natural folded structure of a protein when it is heated or treated with chemicals, after which the protein cannot return to its original form, although its peptide bonds are not broken. The chapter explains it by an activity: when an egg is boiled in water, the protein of the egg white denatures — the soft, clear protein sets into a hard white solid, and this change is permanent.

Q: iv. Describe difference between fats and oils.

Ans: Animal and vegetable fats and oils have similar chemical structures; both are triesters formed from glycerol and long chain organic acids called fatty acids. The degree of unsaturation of the constituent fatty acids determines whether a triglyceride will be a solid or a liquid. Fats are the glycerides in which long chain saturated fatty acid components predominate (e.g. palmitic acid), so they tend to be solid or semisolid. Oils are glycerol esters which contain a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acid components (e.g. oleic acid), so they are liquids. For example, unsaturated mustard oil (sarsoon) remains liquid while saturated bees wax is in the solid state. The melting point of mixed glycerides mainly depends on the number (ratio) of unsaturated fatty acid components in the molecule.

Q: v. Write brief composition of Nucleic acid.

Ans: Each nucleotide of DNA and RNA is composed of the following three components: (1) a sugar — ribose in RNA and deoxyribose in DNA; (2) a nitrogenous base, which is a heterocyclic amine and is either a purine or a pyrimidine; and (3) a phosphate group. Most of the nucleotides are biopolymers of nucleosides and phosphate groups.

mcqs.why: The solved answer states that all carbohydrates are of plant origin except lactose, which is of animal origin, unlike cellulose, starch and sucrose.

mcqs.why: Among the medical uses of carbohydrates, the chapter states that cardiac glycosides are used to normalize heartbeat, while fibres mainly control constipation and diarrhoea.

mcqs.why: The solved answer states clearly that disulfide bridges are found only in sulphur-containing protein molecules, contributing to secondary, tertiary and quaternary structures.

mcqs.why: Fats are glycerides in which long chain saturated fatty acid components predominate, for example palmitic acid, so they tend to be solid or semisolid.

mcqs.why: Oils are glycerol esters containing a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acid components, for example oleic acid, so they remain liquids unlike fats.

mcqs.why: Each nucleotide has a sugar component: ribose in RNA and deoxyribose in DNA, together with a nitrogenous base and a phosphate group.
