lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy derivatives of aldehydes and ketones with general formula Cn(H2O)n, classified as monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides.
  • Monosaccharides cannot be hydrolysed further; polysaccharides contain 100 or more units, are insoluble and tasteless, and are called non-sugars.
  • Proteins are biopolymers of amino acids; the name comes from the Greek word Proteios meaning of prime importance.
  • Haemoglobin carries oxygen, hormones and enzymes regulate the body, and antibodies provide body defence; all are proteins.
  • Lipids are insoluble in water but soluble in ether, chloroform and alcohol; simple lipids are triglycerides such as fats, oils and waxes.
  • Nucleic acids were discovered by Friedrich Miescher; DNA and RNA nucleotides are joined through phosphodiester linkages.
  • Protein synthesis is completed in two stages: transcription and translation.
  • Fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E and K; water-soluble vitamins are B-complex and C, whose deficiency causes scurvy.

Solved Exercises

Exercise Q.3 — Comprehensive questions

Q: i. What are carbohydrates? Explain classification of carbohydrates.

Ans: Carbohydrates are commonly known as 'sugars' and can be defined as polyhydroxy derivatives of aldehydes and ketones. They are polyfunctional (alcohol + aldehyde or ketone) organic compounds containing mainly carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, with the general formula Cn(H2O)n, where n is 3 or greater than 3. Their main function is to support plant structure (cellulose) and to store chemical energy in the form of glycogen and starch.
Classification of carbohydrates:
(1) Monosaccharides: These are the simplest sugars/carbohydrates, which cannot be hydrolysed further. They are colourless, water-soluble organic compounds having a sweet taste and the general formula Cn(H2O)n, where n = 3, 4, 5 and so on. They are either aldoses (having an aldehydic functional group, e.g. glucose) or ketoses (having a ketonic functional group, e.g. fructose). They may be trioses (C3H6O3), tetroses (C4H8O4), pentoses (C5H10O5) and hexoses (C6H12O6).
(2) Oligosaccharides: These are formed when two to nine monosaccharide units combine with each other by the loss of water molecules, resulting in the formation of a glycosidic linkage. On hydrolysis they yield two to nine monosaccharide units. Those consisting of two units are called disaccharides, e.g. maltose (glucose + glucose), lactose (glucose + galactose) and sucrose (glucose + fructose); those containing three units are trisaccharides, e.g. raffinose (C18H32O16).
(3) Polysaccharides: These are biopolymers of monosaccharides having high molecular mass, consisting of 100 or more monosaccharide units joined together through glycosidic linkages, e.g. starch, dextrine, glycogen and cellulose. Hydrolysis of polysaccharides gives many molecules of monosaccharides: (C6H10O5)n + nH2O --H+--> nC6H12O6. They are amorphous solids, insoluble in water and tasteless, and are called 'non-sugars'. They are used as energy storage (glycogen in animals, starch in plants) and as structural units of cells.

Q: ii. Describe proteins, the nature of bonding in protein and their uses.

Ans: Proteins: The name protein is derived from the Greek word 'Proteios' meaning 'of prime importance'. Proteins are biopolymers of amino acids. They are complex nitrogenous compounds present in the living cells of plants and animals, which are essential for growth and maintenance of life. Elements like carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, hydrogen and sulphur are present in proteins. Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins; thus proteins are polyamides formed by the condensation of alpha-amino acids, with a molecular weight greater than 10,000. Examples are globulin, keratin and albumin.
Bonding in proteins: In protein molecules three types of bondings may occur: (i) peptide bondings — amino acids are joined together by peptide linkage by condensation with the removal of a water molecule, giving a linear sequence; (ii) hydrogen bondings; and (iii) disulfide bridges, which are found only in sulphur-containing protein molecules. Due to hydrogen bonding and sulphide bridges, protein molecules get folded and refolded to give secondary, tertiary and quaternary structures. Protein molecules may be fibrous, e.g. keratin in skin and nails, and globular, e.g. haemoglobin and antibodies.
Uses/functions of proteins: (1) Body structures like skin, nails, hair, hoofs, horns and feathers are composed of proteins. (2) As oxygen carrier: haemoglobin, a blood protein, is the main carrier of oxygen to all parts of the body. (3) As body regulators: hormones and enzymes are proteinaceous in nature and are chemical regulators in the body. (4) Commercial uses of enzymes: enzymes are proteins with catalytic function; they turn starch into sugar, help in improving the quality of products such as textiles, detergents, foods and beverages, and vinegar and cheese are produced by the utilization of enzymes in bacteria and yeast. (5) Body defence system: antibodies, which increase the body immune power, are also of protein nature.

Q: iii. Explain lipids with the classification, sources and uses.

Ans: Lipids: The term lipid is derived from the Greek word 'lipose', which means 'fat'. Lipids are naturally occurring organic compounds of animal and plant origin which are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents like ether, chloroform and alcohol. Generally lipids are esters of long chain fatty acids and alcohols; thus the primary building blocks of lipids are fatty acids and alcohols (glycerol). Fats and oils are the most important lipids found in nature.
Classification: (1) Simple lipids: also known as triglycerides; they produce fatty acids and alcohols upon hydrolysis, e.g. fats, oils and waxes. (2) Complex lipids: those lipids which produce fatty acids, alcohols and some other substances upon hydrolysis are known as complex lipids, e.g. phospholipids, glycolipids and sulfolipids.
Sources: Lipids (fats and oils) come from a variety of natural sources like animals, plants and marine organisms. Animal fats are located particularly in adipose tissue; butter and ghee are special types of animal fats obtained from milk. Vegetable oils are chiefly present in seeds and nuts of plants. Marine oils are obtained from sea animals like salmon and whales.
Uses: (1) They are a good source of energy and make the food more palatable. (2) They exert an insulating effect on the nervous system. (3) They are good energy reservoirs in the body. (4) Lipids are an integral part of cell protoplasm and plasma membrane. (5) Some lipids act as precursors of very important physiological compounds, e.g. cholesterol is the precursor of steroid hormones.

Q: iv. What are Nucleic acids? Describe their types, composition and functions.

Ans: Nucleic acids: Nucleic acids were first discovered in the nuclei of pus cells in 1868 and in sperm heads in 1872 by Friedrich Miescher. They are found in every living cell as well as in viruses and have been found to be the essential components of genes. Their structure contains the blueprints for the normal growth and development of each and every living organism. They are complex biomolecules composed of units called nucleotides.
Types: Naturally occurring nucleic acids are of two types: (i) deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and (ii) ribonucleic acid (RNA).
Composition: Each nucleotide is composed of three components: (1) a sugar — ribose in RNA and deoxyribose in DNA; (2) a nitrogenous base, a heterocyclic amine which is either a purine or a pyrimidine; and (3) a phosphate group. The nucleotides are joined together through phosphodiester linkages.
Functions: (1) Genetic information: Nucleic acids have the ability to reproduce, store and transmit genetic information. The genetic information for the cell is contained in the form of specific codes in DNA molecules. These informations are translated and expressed by the synthesis of specific proteins, which perform various functions in the cell according to the directions given by the codes in DNA. Protein synthesis in the cell is completed in two stages, i.e. transcription and translation. (2) Mutation: Mutation is a sudden chemical change in a DNA molecule that could lead to the synthesis of proteins with an altered amino acid sequence. Changes in DNA molecules may be caused by mutagens like radiations, chemical agents or viruses. The majority of changes in DNA are repaired by special enzymes in the cell; failure in repair by the enzyme system can cause a mutation.

Q: v. What are vitamins and how are they classified?

Ans: Vitamins: Vitamins are organic compounds that cannot be synthesized by an organism but are very essential for the maintenance of normal metabolism, and therefore must be included in the diet. The absence or deficiency of vitamins in the diet results in various diseases. The name was originally 'vitamine', because the first one found was an amine, hence 'vital amine'; later studies showed that they were not all amines, so the 'e' was dropped.
Classification: Vitamins are of two main types:
(1) Fat soluble vitamins: Vitamins A, D, E and K. Vitamin A is obtained from green vegetables and fruits, fish liver oil, eggs, butter and cheese; it combines with the protein opsin to produce the light-absorbing compound rhodopsine, and its deficiency causes night blindness. Vitamin D (calciferol) is found in fish liver oils, milk and butter; it helps in the absorption of calcium and phosphate and its deficiency produces rickets. Vitamin E (tocopherols) is found in vegetable oil, corn oil, soyabean oil, egg yolk and liver; it is used as an antioxidant and its deficiency causes anaemia. Vitamin K, found in cabbage, cauliflower, spinach, tomatoes, cheese, meat and egg yolk, is a factor related to blood clotting, and its deficiency causes haemorrhage.
(2) Water soluble vitamins: Vitamin B-complex and vitamin C. Vitamin B is not a single vitamin but consists of B1, B2, B3, B6, B12 etc. Vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency produces beriberi; vitamin B2 (riboflavin) deficiency causes inflammation of lips and burning of eyes; vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency causes anaemia. Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is mainly obtained from citrus fruits such as lemon and orange, and its deficiency causes scurvy, characterized by pain in joints and bleeding from gums.

mcqs.why: Polysaccharides are amorphous solids, insoluble in water and tasteless, and are called non-sugars. They consist of 100 or more monosaccharide units joined by glycosidic linkages.

mcqs.why: The chapter states the name protein is derived from the Greek word Proteios meaning of prime importance, because proteins are essential for growth and maintenance of life.

mcqs.why: Simple lipids are also known as triglycerides, for example fats, oils and waxes, while phospholipids, glycolipids and sulfolipids are complex lipids.

mcqs.why: Nucleic acids were first discovered in the nuclei of pus cells in 1868 and in sperm heads in 1872 by Friedrich Miescher, according to the chapter.

mcqs.why: The genetic information in DNA is expressed by synthesis of specific proteins, and protein synthesis in the cell is completed in two stages: transcription and translation.

mcqs.why: Vitamin A combines with opsin to produce rhodopsine for vision, and its deficiency causes night blindness. Rickets is from vitamin D and scurvy from vitamin C deficiency.

mcqs.why: Vitamin C is obtained from citrus fruits such as lemon and orange, and its deficiency causes scurvy, characterized by pain in joints and bleeding from gums.

lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Nitrogen is the major component of the troposphere, and air is 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Environmental chemistry is the study of the environment and the changes occurring in it; the environment comprises lithosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere and atmosphere.
  • The stratosphere extends from 11 km to 50 km, is also called the ozonosphere, and ozone concentration is maximum at 30 km.
  • In the stratosphere temperature increases from -56°C to -2°C because ozone absorbs UV radiations, protecting living organisms.
  • Acid rain attacks limestone and marble: CaCO3 + H2SO4 -> CaSO4 + CO2 + H2O, and the soluble CaSO4 is washed away.
  • The atmosphere absorbs cosmic rays, maintains heat balance, allows visible radiations, supplies life gases and carries water from oceans to land.
  • Ozone is bluish, has a characteristic smell, liquefies at -112.4°C and causes rubber to harden and crack.
  • Primary pollutants are released directly into air, e.g. CO2, NO2 and SO2; secondary pollutants are derived from them, e.g. photochemical smog and acid rain.

Solved Exercises

Exercise Q.2 — Write short answers

Q: i. What is environmental chemistry?

Ans: The branch of chemistry which deals with the study of the environment and the changes occurring in it is termed as environmental chemistry. The environment is composed of lithosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere and atmosphere.

Q: ii. Write short note on stratosphere.

Ans: The stratosphere is the second layer of the atmosphere, which is above the troposphere. It extends from 11 km to 50 km. The major component of the stratosphere is ozone (O3), therefore it is also called the 'ozonosphere'. The concentration of ozone increases with the increase of height and is maximum at 30 km. The stratosphere shows a positive lapse rate, because the temperature increases from -56°C to -2°C with height; this increase in temperature is due to the presence of ozone, which absorbs the UV radiations of the sun. The stratosphere absorbs UV radiations, thus protecting living organisms on the earth surface from the harmful effects of UV radiations.

Q: iii. Effect of acid rain on building materials.

Ans: Acid rain causes extensive damage to buildings and sculptures and other things made of limestone and marble, as:
CaCO3 + H2SO4 -> CaSO4 + CO2 + H2O
The CaSO4 formed is soluble in water and is washed away with rain water, so the buildings and statues are gradually damaged. The deformation of historical statues in Greece and Italy was reported to be due to acid rain, and the Taj Mahal in India faces the same fate at present.

Q: iv. What is the importance of atmosphere?

Ans: The atmosphere plays an important role for living organisms: (1) It protects the earth by absorbing the dangerous cosmic rays of the sun. (2) It plays a role in maintaining the heat balance of the earth by absorbing the heat radiations re-emitted by the earth surface. (3) It allows visible radiations coming from the sun, as a result of which we can see. (4) It is the main source of different gases which are important for life, i.e. oxygen, which is essential for life on earth; carbon dioxide is essential for plant photosynthesis and nitrogen is a useful macronutrient for plants. (5) It is a vital carrier of water from oceans to land, which is very important for the hydrological cycle.

Q: v. List the physical properties of ozone.

Ans: The physical properties (characteristics) of ozone are: (i) It is bluish in colour. (ii) It has a characteristic smell. (iii) It is a respiratory irritant if present in excess in air. (iv) Ozone is soluble in water, turpentine oil, glacial acetic acid and carbon tetrachloride. (v) It can be liquefied at -112.4°C, and the liquid has a pale blue colour. (vi) Ozone causes rubber to harden and crack.

Q: vi. What are primary and secondary air pollutants?

Ans: Major air pollutants are of two types. (i) Primary pollutants: those pollutants which are released directly into the air are called primary pollutants, e.g. CO2, NO2 and SO2 etc. (ii) Secondary pollutants: those pollutants which have their origin in the primary pollutants and are derived from them are called secondary pollutants, e.g. photochemical smog and acid rain etc.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The atmosphere is 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and 0.03% CO2, with mass about 4.5 to 5 x 10^15 metric tonnes and total height about 500 km.
  • The troposphere is the lowest layer, about 11 km high, where weather phenomena occur; the thermosphere extends from 85 km to 500 km.
  • Air pollution is the release of substances in sufficient concentration to cause harmful effects to human beings, vegetation and other living things (WHO).
  • About 75% of carbon monoxide emission results from automobiles; natural sources release 800-2000 million tonnes of particulate matter per year.
  • Ozone depletion is the decrease of stratospheric ozone below its normal level; CFCs are the main compounds responsible.
  • Ozone is depleted by NOx (NO + O3 -> NO2 + O2), by atomic oxygen (O3 + O -> 2O2) and by oxides of sulphur.
  • Acid rain has pH less than 5.6; SO3 + H2O -> H2SO4 and N2O5 + H2O -> 2HNO3 are formed in rain water.
  • A 1% decrease in ozone causes a 5% increase in skin cancer; UV radiations penetrate water about 20 m and kill microorganisms.

Solved Exercises

Exercise Q.3 — Write long answers

Q: i. Explain the composition and layers of atmosphere.

Ans: Composition of atmosphere: The atmosphere is the protective blanket of air around the earth surface. It is a mixture of different gases like N2, O2, CO2 and Ar etc. The major constituents of the atmosphere are N2 and O2, while its minor constituents are CO2 and Ar (argon) and some trace gases. Air consists of 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and 0.03% CO2. The mass of the atmosphere is approximately 4.5 to 5 x 10^15 metric tonnes. Its temperature ranges from -92°C to 1200°C and changes with altitude; the pressure is 1 atm at sea level and decreases to 3 x 10^-7 atm at about 100 km above sea level. The density of the atmosphere is 0.0013 g/cm^3, which gradually decreases with altitude. The atmosphere absorbs the dangerous cosmic and UV radiations coming from the sun and so sustains life on earth.
Layers of atmosphere: The total height of the atmosphere from the earth surface is about 500 km. On the basis of temperature and density it is divided into four layers:
(1) Troposphere: It is the lowest layer, close to the earth surface, with an average height of about 11 km (16 km at the equator). Most weather phenomena and cloud formation take place in it. Its temperature range is from 60°C to -56°C and it shows a negative lapse rate. Its major components are N2, O2, CO2 and H2O vapours, and it constitutes about 70% of the atmosphere.
(2) Stratosphere: It is the second layer, extending from 11 km to 50 km. Its major component is ozone (O3), so it is also called the ozonosphere; ozone concentration is maximum at 30 km. It shows a positive lapse rate, the temperature increasing from -56°C to -2°C with height, because ozone absorbs UV radiations.
(3) Mesosphere: It is the third layer, from 50 km to 85 km. Its major components are O3+ and NO+. The temperature decreases from -2°C to -92°C with increasing height, due to the low level of UV-absorbing species like O3.
(4) Thermosphere: It is the fourth zone, from 85 km to 500 km. The temperature increases from -92°C to 1200°C with height (positive lapse rate), because gases absorb UV radiations and undergo ionization, e.g. O2 --hv--> O2+ + e-. Its important components are O2+, NO+ and O+; due to the presence of ions it is also called the ionosphere.

Q: ii. What is air pollution? Explain the major sources of air pollution.

Ans: Air pollution (according to the World Health Organization, WHO) may be defined as: 'The substances released to air either by human activities or by natural activities, in sufficient concentration to cause harmful effects to human beings, vegetation and other living things.' Air consists of 21% oxygen, 78% nitrogen and 0.03% CO2; if these gases are present in more or less concentration than the given values, they will be harmful for living organisms and thus act as pollutants.
Major sources of air pollution:
(A) Sources of particulate pollutants (small particles of liquids and solids): (1) Natural sources: volcanic eruption, soil erosion by wind, dust storms, natural forest fires and salt spray from oceans; natural sources release about 800-2000 million tonnes of particulate matter per year. (2) Anthropogenic (man-made) sources: combustion of fuels and wood, construction, mountain blasting, mining and other industrial processes, releasing about 200-400 million tonnes per year; the most common are fly ash from power plants and smelters and smoke from incomplete combustion processes.
(B) Sources of gaseous pollutants (CFC, CO, NO, NO2, SO2 etc.): (1) Carbon monoxide: natural sources are volcanic eruptions, natural gas emission, electrical discharges during storms, seed germination and marsh gas production. Most CO production results from human activities: about 75% of CO emission results from automobiles due to internal combustion engines, forest fires contribute 16.9%, iron and steel industries 9.6% and agricultural burning 7.2%; cigarette smoke also contains a fairly high concentration of CO. (2) Oxides of nitrogen (N2O, NO2, NO): natural sources are soil, bacteria and other microorganisms (e.g. pseudomonas bacteria convert atmospheric N2 gas into oxides of nitrogen), releasing about 5 x 10^8 tonnes of NOx per year; man-made sources are automobiles, industries, furnaces, thermal power plants and, most importantly, jet engine aeroplanes. (3) Sulphur oxides (SO2, SO3): natural sources contribute 67% of total SOx emission — volcanic eruptions, rock weathering, sulphate spray from oceans and other biological activities, which emit SO2 or H2S (2H2S + 3O2 -> 2SO2 + 2H2O). Man-made sources contribute about 33%, mainly the combustion of fossil fuels (coal and oil) contaminated with sulphur, industries (22%) and transportation (2%).

Q: iii. What is ozone depletion? Write its mechanism.

Ans: Ozone depletion: The decrease in the concentration of ozone in the stratosphere below its normal or natural level is termed 'ozone depletion'; the formation of a hole in the ozonosphere (ozone layer) is also called ozone depletion. It results from human activities as well as natural phenomena which release many pollutants and other chemical species into the atmosphere; these species react with the ozone layer in the stratosphere and decrease its concentration. Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) are the main lethal compounds implicated in the accelerated depletion of the ozone layer; they originate from industrial, commercial and household appliances. The ozone layer is also destroyed by chlorine released due to volcanic activity.
Mechanism of ozone depletion:
(1) Due to NOx: The oxides of nitrogen (NO, N2O and NO2) react with ozone photochemically and cause its depletion: NO + O3 -> NO2 + O2.
(2) Due to atomic (nascent) oxygen: Atomic oxygen is produced by the reaction O2 --hv--> O + O. This atomic oxygen consumes about 18% of the O3 found in the atmosphere: O3 + O -> 2O2.
(3) Due to oxides of sulphur: SO2 may undergo a photochemical reaction with O3 and cause its dissociation: SO2 --hv--> SO2 (excited); SO2 + O3 -> SO3 + O2.

Q: iv. Discuss acid rain. How does it affect environment?

Ans: Acid rain: Normal rain water is slightly acidic because of dissolved CO2 and has a pH of 5.6 (CO2 + H2O -> H2CO3, carbonic acid). Rain having pH less than 5.6 is called acid rain; rain with a pH as low as 2.1 has been reported, which is lower than the pH of vinegar and lemon juice. In common language, acid rain means excessive acid in rain water, and it is one of the adverse effects of air pollution.
Mechanism: Energy sources like coal, wood and oil contain sulphur, nitrogen and other hydrocarbons. When these fuels are burnt in air they are converted into their respective oxides, SOx and NOx. These oxides are highly soluble in rain water and produce different acids: SOx are converted to H2SO4 (2SO2 + O2 -> 2SO3; SO3 + H2O -> H2SO4) and NOx to HNO3 (NO + O3 -> NO2 + O2; NO2 + O3 -> NO3 + O2; NO2 + NO3 -> N2O5; N2O5 + H2O -> 2HNO3). The organic compounds are oxidized to CH3COOH.
Effects of acid rain on the environment:
(1) On humans: Acid rain mainly causes damage to lungs, skin and hair. The heavy metals released by acid rain may also cause a potential threat to human health, and acid rain increases the acidity of water, which gives rise to water-borne diseases.
(2) On plants: It destroys the leaves of plants; young plants, specially the newly growing buds and tips, are seriously damaged, so the growth of plants is affected.
(3) On soil: Acid rain increases the acidity of soil and thus affects the availability of plant nutrients.
(4) On aquatic life: Aquatic life such as fishes, plants and other microorganisms is very sensitive to acidity and is greatly damaged; pollutants entering rivers and lakes when snow melts destroy fish eggs at the time of fish spawning and hatching.
(5) On materials: Acid rain causes extensive damage to buildings and sculptures made of limestone and marble: CaCO3 + H2SO4 -> CaSO4 + CO2 + H2O; the CaSO4 is soluble in water and is washed away.

Q: v. How does ozone depletion adversely affect our life?

Ans: Both living organisms (plants and animals) as well as materials are greatly affected by ozone depletion, because cosmic rays and UV radiations then reach the earth surface.
(1) Effect on humans and animals: In minor cases these radiations cause sunburn disease, but in major cases they damage the skin tissues and cause skin cancer, which kills about 12,000 people each year in the USA; it has been estimated that a 1% decrease in ozone causes a 5% increase in skin cancer. These radiations also cause an eye disease known as 'cataracts'; about 12 million people have become blind due to this disease and about 18 million have lost a part of their eyesight. It also causes pulmonary edema and even death. Pink eye and eye cancer cases are also found in cattle exposed to UV radiations.
(2) Effect on marine life: The cosmic and UV radiations are highly energetic; they penetrate water (about 20 m) and kill the microorganisms present in water, which are more sensitive to these radiations.
(3) Effect on crops: Ozone depletion causes an adverse effect on the production of crops; it has been estimated that a 25% increase in UV radiation decreases soya bean crop product by 25%. UV radiation also affects young tobacco and tomato crops.
(4) Effect on materials: With the decrease in the ozone layer, the UV radiations reaching the earth surface increase and thus reduce the lifetime of commonly used synthetic materials like plastics, cotton, nylon and Styrofoam. Ozone causes rubber to harden and crack, thus shortening the life of automobile tyres and other rubber items. Due to ozone depletion, the temperature of the earth surface increases and causes 'global warming'.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Coastal temperatures stay moderate because water has a very high specific heat and acts as a giant thermostat.
  • Ice floats because hexagonal structures with empty spaces lower its density to 0.917 g/ml at 0°C.
  • H2O is liquid at room temperature while H2S is a gas because of hydrogen bonding in water.
  • Water is a universal solvent because of its polarity and its high dielectric constant of 80 at 18°C.
  • Ammonium chloride solution is acidic because it is a salt of a weak base NH4OH and a strong acid HCl and hydrolyses.
  • Boiling drinking water kills pathogens such as bacteria, viruses and protozoans.
  • Eutrophication is nutrient enrichment of water bodies that causes algal overgrowth and dead zones.
  • Leachate forms when rain water dissolves chemicals from solid waste, and thermal pollution lowers dissolved oxygen in water.

Solved Exercises

Exercise Q.2 — Give brief answers to each of the following questions

Q: i. Why the temperatures of the coastal areas remain moderate throughout the year?

Ans: Water has a very high specific heat (4.2 J/g/°C), so the water of oceans and seas near the coastal areas absorbs and releases heat very slowly and undergoes temperature changes very slowly as compared to land. The vast amount of water therefore acts as a giant thermostat and regulates the temperature, keeping the temperature of the coastal areas moderate throughout the year.

Q: ii. Why ice floats on the surface of water?

Ans: When water is cooled below 4°C, its density gradually decreases, reaching 0.917 g/ml at 0°C, where it freezes into ice. This expansion of ice is due to the formation of hexagonal structures, in which six water molecules arrange themselves in the form of a ring having empty spaces; as a result the volume increases and the density decreases. Thus ice is lighter than water and therefore floats on the surface of water.

Q: iii. Why H2O is liquid at room temperature while H2S is gas?

Ans: The unusual physical properties of water are due to hydrogen bonding in it. Because of hydrogen bonding, the melting and boiling points of water (0°C and 100°C) are unexpectedly high as compared to the other chemically similar hydrides of Group VI-A — H2S is a gas with boiling point -60°C and has no hydrogen bonding. So H2O is liquid at room temperature while H2S is a gas.

Q: iv. How the enormous quantity of water present on earth surface acts as a giant thermostat?

Ans: The specific heat capacity of water is very high: one gram of water requires 4.2 joules of heat to raise its temperature by one degree centigrade, much higher than many other common substances. Due to this high specific heat, water undergoes temperature changes very slowly. The vast amount of water on the earth surface therefore acts as a giant thermostat and regulates the temperature of the earth; without the huge volume of water in the oceans, the earth would have heated up too much quickly during the day time and cooled too much quickly at night.

Q: v. Why water has soothing effect on the body in summer?

Ans: The latent heat of vaporization of water is very high, 41 kJ/mol (2277 kJ/kg) at 100°C. When water (or sweat) evaporates from the body in summer, it absorbs a large amount of heat from the body for this change of state, so the body is cooled and feels a soothing effect. Due to high latent heat values, water is also a useful coolant.

Q: vi. Why water is a universal solvent? Explain.

Ans: Water is called a universal solvent because it has the ability to dissolve more or less of everything, due to two reasons. (1) Polarity: water molecules have a polar structure; the oxygen end is partially negatively charged while the hydrogen end is partially positively charged, so polar substances like mineral acids, bases and salts dissolve in water, and covalent compounds having hydroxyl groups, e.g. glucose, sugar and alcohols, also dissolve. When an ionic compound like NaCl is placed in water, the water molecules orient their negative poles towards the positive ions and their positive poles around the negative ions, breaking the ionic bonds. (2) Dielectric constant: water has a high dielectric constant of 80 at 18°C, so the force of attraction between the positive and negative ions of a dissolved salt becomes very small and the ions remain separated and soluble.

Q: vii. The aqueous solution of ammonium chloride is acidic. Why?

Ans: The reaction of a salt of a weak acid or weak base with water to form an acidic or basic solution is called hydrolysis; in this reaction water splits into H+ and OH- ions, and it is the reverse process of neutralization. Ammonium chloride is a salt of a weak base (NH4OH) and a strong acid (HCl), so it hydrolyses as:
NH4Cl(s) + H2O(l) -> NH4OH(aq) + HCl(aq)
The solution therefore becomes acidic.

Q: viii. Why fire starts burning on the surface of water, when a piece of sodium metal is put into it?

Ans: Cold water reacts vigorously with sodium, forming sodium hydroxide and liberating hydrogen gas:
2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) -> 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g)
The reaction is so vigorous and produces so much heat that the liberated hydrogen gas catches fire, so fire starts burning on the surface of water.

Q: ix. Explain why it is advisable to drink boiled water.

Ans: Untreated water, especially water contaminated by sewage, contains pathogens such as bacteria, viruses and protozoans, which cause water-borne diseases like typhoid, cholera, dysentery, amoebiasis, ascariasis and hepatitis. Boiling the water kills these disease-causing microorganisms, so it is advisable to drink boiled water to remain safe from these diseases.

Q: x. Water extinguishes the burning coal. How both can be used as fuel?

Ans: Water extinguishes burning coal because, due to its high heat capacity and high latent heat of vaporization, it absorbs a large amount of heat and cools the coal below its ignition temperature. But both can be used as fuel together: when steam is passed over red-hot coke (coal), it forms a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen gases called water gas, which is used as a fuel:
H2O(g) + C(s) -> CO(g) + H2(g) (water gas)

Q: xi. What is Eutrophication? How does it pollute water?

Ans: Eutrophication is the enrichment of nutrients in water bodies. The discharges of nitrogen, phosphorus and other nutrients come from agriculture, waste disposal, coastal development and fossil fuel. This enrichment stimulates the harmful overgrowth of algae, which can have a direct toxic effect, as certain types of algae are toxic (red and brown). Zooplankton eat the toxic algae and begin passing the toxins up the food chain, affecting sea birds, sea mammals and humans, causing illness and sometimes death. The algal growth also blocks the sunlight needed by sea grasses and reduces the clarity of water. When the algae finally die, they sink to the bottom and begin decomposing; this process uses oxygen from the surrounding water and makes it difficult for aquatic animals to survive, and the region becomes a dead zone.

Q: xii. What are the effects of chemical contamination?

Ans: The major effects of chemical contamination are: (i) Pesticides affect and damage the nervous system, liver, reproductive system and endocrine glands and DNA; they also cause cancer and other acutely toxic and chronic effects. (ii) Oil and petrochemicals can alter the ecology of aquatic habitats and the physiology of marine organisms; in human beings they cause gastrointestinal irritation, liver and kidney damage and nervous system effects. (iii) Mercury enters water bodies through air pollution and industrial waste and gets into the body through food, especially sea food; it accumulates in the blood, liver, kidneys and brain tissues. In young children it causes autism, brain damage, learning defects and incomplete mental development; in adults it causes Parkinson's, Alzheimer's disease and heart disease. (iv) Persistent organic pollutants (POPs) such as DDT, dioxins and PCB enter the body through food; being fat soluble, they accumulate in the fatty tissues of animals and humans, cause disruption of hormones, affect reproductive organs and cause breast cancer in women.

Q: xiii. Why chlorine acts as bleaching agent in the presence of water?

Ans: When Cl2 gas is passed through water, it reacts to form hydrochloric (HCl) and hypochlorous (HOCl) acids:
H2O(l) + Cl2(g) -> HCl(aq) + HOCl(aq)
Hypochlorous acid is unstable and decomposes to give atomic oxygen:
HOCl(aq) -> HCl(aq) + [O]
This atomic oxygen decolourizes the dye molecule, so chlorine acts as a bleaching agent in the presence of water; it is also used as a germicide.

Q: xiv. What is leachate? How does it gets dissolved in water?

Ans: Solid waste (urban or domestic waste) stored in open fields contains many chemicals. When rain water is filtered through this material, the chemicals dissolve into the rain water; this process is called leaching and the resulting mixture is called leachate. Leachate contains decomposed organic matter, rust, newspaper ink, pesticides, fertilizer and other hazardous chemicals. It either seeps into the soil and pollutes underground water or finds its way to rivers and streams through rain water.

Q: xv. What is thermal pollution? How does it affect the aquatic life?

Ans: Thermal pollution is caused when hot water discharged from power plants and industries enters water bodies. A lot of heat is generated in most industrial manufacturing processes, and the cheapest way to release it is to draw water from a nearby source, pass it through the plant and return the heated water back into the same source. The warmer water affects aquatic life in two ways: (i) it decreases the solubility of oxygen, and many aquatic organisms die due to the shortage of oxygen; (ii) many aquatic animals, especially the young, cannot survive above 30°C and die.

options: Water has a very low specific heat, so it heats up and cools down very quickly
Water has a very high specific heat, so it absorbs and releases heat very slowly and changes temperature slowly compared with land
Water freezes at 0°C and keeps the coast cold throughout the year
Hydrogen bonding stops water from absorbing any heat from the sun
mcqs.why: Water has a very high specific heat of 4.2 J/g/°C, so ocean and sea water near coastal areas absorbs and releases heat very slowly. The vast amount of water acts as a giant thermostat and keeps coastal temperatures moderate.

options: Ice contains trapped air bubbles that always make it lighter than liquid water
Ice is made of a different substance that is lighter than water
The density of water increases below 4°C, pushing the ice up to the surface
On freezing, water forms hexagonal structures with empty spaces, so its volume increases and its density falls to 0.917 g/ml at 0°C, making ice lighter than water
mcqs.why: When water is cooled below 4 degrees C its density gradually decreases, reaching 0.917 g/ml at 0 degrees C where it freezes. The expansion is due to hexagonal structures of six water molecules with empty spaces, so ice is lighter and floats.

Water contains ionic bonds while H2S contains only weak covalent bonds
H2S dissolves completely in air at room temperature
mcqs.why: The unusual properties of water are due to hydrogen bonding, so its melting point 0 degrees C and boiling point 100 degrees C are unexpectedly high. H2S has no hydrogen bonding and is a gas with boiling point minus 60 degrees C.

Water in the body freezes and lowers the body temperature
Its latent heat of vaporization is very high, so evaporating sweat absorbs a large amount of heat from the body
Its density is maximum at 4°C, which cools the body

Because it has a very high boiling point of 100°C
Because of its polarity and its high dielectric constant of 80 at 18°C, it dissolves more or less of everything
Because it contains dissolved gases and salts from nature

Ammonium chloride is a salt of a strong base and a weak acid
Water itself becomes acidic whenever any salt is dissolved in it

Water decomposes into oxygen which makes the sodium burn
Sodium reacts with water to form petrol which catches fire
Sodium reacts vigorously with cold water forming NaOH and hydrogen gas, and the heat produced makes the hydrogen catch fire
mcqs.why: Cold water reacts vigorously with sodium: 2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) gives 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g). The reaction produces so much heat that the liberated hydrogen gas catches fire, so fire starts burning on the surface of water.

options: Boiling removes all dissolved salts and makes water pure
Boiling kills the pathogens such as bacteria, viruses and protozoans present in contaminated water
Boiling adds useful minerals to the drinking water
Boiling converts hard water permanently into soft water

Burning coal melts ice and the steam pressure runs an engine directly
Water dissolves coal to form a liquid fuel that burns slowly
Coal absorbs water and then burns for a much longer time

The enrichment of nutrients in water bodies, which stimulates the harmful overgrowth of algae

Decomposition uses up oxygen from the surrounding water, making it difficult for aquatic animals to survive, and the region becomes a dead zone
The dead algae form a layer of ice on the water surface
The toxins are destroyed and the water becomes safe for drinking

Water that is left after the fractional distillation of petroleum

lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Water density rises to a maximum of 1.000 g/ml at 4°C and falls to 0.917 g/ml at 0°C, so ice floats.
  • The specific heat capacity of water, 4.2 J/g/°C, is much higher than ethanol, iron, copper and mercury.
  • Steam over red hot iron gives Fe3O4 and hydrogen, and hydrolysis of CH3COONa gives CH3COOH and NaOH.
  • Industrial waste contains toxic compounds of mercury, cadmium, lead, chromium, arsenic and antimony.
  • Untreated sewage is black water and the major source of water pollution, while kitchen and washroom waste water is grey water.
  • Water-borne diseases include typhoid, cholera, dysentery, amoebiasis, ascariasis and hepatitis.
  • Persistent organic pollutants accumulate in fatty tissues and disrupt hormones.
  • The taste of drinking water is due to dissolved gases and salts, and bicarbonates, sulphates and chlorides of calcium and magnesium make water hard.

Solved Exercises

Exercise Q.3 — Comprehensive questions

Q: i. Describe the physical properties of water.

Ans: (i) Physical state: Pure water is colourless (transparent), odourless and tasteless. The taste of drinking water is due to the presence of dissolved gases and salts. Water exists in nature in all three states, i.e. solid (ice), liquid and gaseous (vapour).
(ii) Melting point and boiling point: Under normal atmospheric pressure, liquid water changes into solid ice at 0°C and boils to form steam at 100°C. The melting and boiling points of water are unexpectedly high as compared to other chemically similar compounds (H2S: m.p. -83°C, b.p. -60°C; H2Se: -66°C, -41°C; H2Te: -49°C, -2°C). This and other unusual properties of water are due to hydrogen bonding in it.
(iii) Density: Water shows a unique property called the anomalous behaviour of water. When water is cooled from 100°C, its density gradually increases from 0.9584 g/ml to 1.000 g/ml at 4°C. On further cooling below 4°C the effect reverses and the density gradually decreases, reaching 0.917 g/ml at 0°C, where water freezes into ice. Thus ice is lighter and floats on the surface of water. The expansion of ice is due to the formation of hexagonal structures with empty spaces. As water expands on freezing, bottles filled with water crack in the freezer, and water supply pipes may burst during severe winters.
(iv) Heat capacity: The specific heat capacity of water is 4.2 J/g/°C, much higher than ethanol (2.4), iron (0.45), copper (0.376) and mercury (0.1). Due to its high specific heat, water undergoes temperature changes very slowly; it is used in radiators for heating rooms, and the vast amount of water on the earth surface acts as a giant thermostat regulating the temperature of the earth.
(v) Latent heat values: The latent heat of fusion of water is 6 kJ/mol (334 kJ/kg), and its latent heat of vaporization is 41 kJ/mol (2277 kJ/kg) at 100°C. Due to high latent heat values, water is a useful coolant.
(vi) Solvent action: Water is a remarkable solvent; it has the ability to dissolve many substances and is therefore termed the universal solvent.

Q: ii. Write balanced chemical equations for the chemical reactions of water with the following: (a) K (b) Ca (c) Zn (d) Fe (e) Cl2 (f) C (g) Na2O (h) NO2 (i) CH3COONa

Ans: (a) With K: 2K(s) + 2H2O(l) -> 2KOH(aq) + H2(g)
(b) With Ca: Ca(s) + 2H2O(l) -> Ca(OH)2(aq) + H2(g)
(c) With Zn (steam): Zn(s) + H2O -> ZnO(s) + H2(g)
(d) With Fe (steam over red hot iron): 3Fe(s) + 4H2O(g) -> Fe3O4(s) + 4H2(g)
(e) With Cl2: H2O(l) + Cl2(g) -> HCl(aq) + HOCl(aq)
(f) With C (steam over red-hot coke): H2O(g) + C(s) -> CO(g) + H2(g) (water gas)
(g) With Na2O: Na2O(s) + H2O(l) -> 2NaOH(aq)
(h) With NO2: H2O(l) + 2NO2(g) -> HNO3(aq) + HNO2(aq)
(i) With CH3COONa (hydrolysis): CH3COONa(s) + H2O(l) -> CH3COOH(aq) + NaOH(aq)

Q: iii. Discuss the following: (a) Industrial wastes (b) Household wastes

Ans: (a) Industrial wastes: As populations and production grew, industrial and household refuse accumulated, and many discarded materials did not simply disappear but were spread through the water table, absorbed by lower forms of life and passed into the food chain, causing deaths, birth defects and mental problems. Water pollution is a serious problem in developing nations, which have high populations and manufacturing facilities that do not meet safety standards; most industries have been started without proper planning and waste treatment plants, and they just dispose of untreated toxic waste into nearby drains, canals or rivers. Manufacturing and service industries have high demands of water for cooling, processing and cleaning; most of it is taken from the adjoining river, canal, stream or underground source and again discharged into these sources laden with toxic wastes. Industrial waste contains highly toxic compounds of mercury, cadmium, lead, chromium, arsenic and antimony; in addition it also contains acids, bases, dyes, oils and grease.
(b) Household wastes: Household waste is the waste generated in the day-to-day operations of a household, from lawn clippings to burnt-out light bulbs. It is broadly divided into three categories. (1) Waste water or grey water: the water used in kitchens, washrooms and cleaning floors, directly discharged into water bodies; modern synthetic detergents and washing powders contain phosphates, and chemicals like medicines, acids, bleaches, dyes, insecticides, rodent killers, waxes and hair colour affect the health of all forms of life in the water. (2) Untreated sewage or black water: the major source of water pollution, because it contains pathogens such as bacteria, viruses and protozoans; in Pakistan about 2 million tonnes of wet human excreta are annually produced in the urban sector, of which about 50% go into water bodies, and about 40% of deaths are related to water-borne diseases. (3) Solid waste: urban or domestic waste in solid or semisolid form — food, newspapers, glass bottles, cans, metals etc. — dumped into streams, lakes, rivers and seas, or stored in open fields; chemicals from it dissolve into rain water by leaching, forming leachate, which pollutes underground water and rivers.

Q: iv. Describe in detail the effects of water pollutants on life.

Ans: The effects of water pollutants are devastating not only to people but also to animals, fish and birds. Polluted water is unsuitable for drinking, recreation, agriculture and industry; it diminishes the aesthetic quality of lakes and rivers, destroys aquatic life and reduces its reproductive ability, and is a hazard to human health. The major effects are:
(a) Infectious diseases: Water-borne diseases occur when parasites or other disease-causing microorganisms are transmitted via contaminated water, particularly water contaminated by pathogens originating from excreta. These include typhoid, cholera, dysentery, amoebiasis, ascariasis and hepatitis.
(b) Nutrient pollution (eutrophication): Discharges of nitrogen, phosphorus and other nutrients from agriculture, waste disposal, coastal development and fossil fuel enrich water bodies and stimulate harmful overgrowth of algae, some of which are toxic. The toxins pass up the food chain to sea birds, sea mammals and humans; algal growth blocks sunlight needed by sea grasses, and when the algae die and decompose, they use up the oxygen of the water, making the region a dead zone.
(c) Chemical contamination: Pesticides damage the nervous system, liver, reproductive system, endocrine glands and DNA and cause cancer. Oil and petrochemicals alter the ecology of aquatic habitats and cause gastrointestinal irritation, liver and kidney damage in humans. Mercury accumulates in the blood, liver, kidneys and brain tissues, causing autism and brain damage in young children and Parkinson's, Alzheimer's and heart disease in adults. Persistent organic pollutants (DDT, dioxins, PCB) accumulate in fatty tissues and disrupt hormones.
(d) Thermal water pollution: Heated water returned by industries decreases the solubility of oxygen, so many aquatic organisms die due to shortage of oxygen, and many aquatic animals, especially the young, cannot survive above 30°C.

Q: v. Water is an excellent solvent. Explain how this property is beneficial for life but sometimes a nuisance for us.

Ans: Water is a universal solvent for many inorganic and certain organic compounds. This property is due to its polarity and its high dielectric constant (80 at 18°C), because of which it dissolves more or less of everything.
Beneficial for life: This property is very beneficial for us and finds a large number of applications at home and in industry. Water present in springs, streams, rivers, lakes and seas dissolves useful minerals; the taste of drinking water is due to dissolved gases and salts. The vital function of protoplasm is due to the presence of a constant amount of water, and living bodies (the human body contains about 70% water) depend on water to dissolve and carry substances needed for biological processes.
A nuisance: However, the same property of water is responsible for water pollution as well. Because water dissolves a vast variety of substances, natural water, as it flows or seeps through the surface of the earth, dissolves minerals, salts and other substances, and man-made chemicals also get dissolved in water and make it harmful for humans, animals and plants. Water is considered polluted and unfit for drinking when it is contaminated with pollutants such as human or animal waste, disease-producing organisms, radioactive material, toxic metals like lead or mercury and agricultural chemicals such as pesticides, herbicides and fertilizers. The dissolved bicarbonates, sulphates and chlorides of calcium and magnesium also make water hard, which wastes soap and harms boilers and health.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Metallurgy is the art and science of making metals and alloys from their ores; its operations are concentration, roasting, reduction and refining.
  • An ore is an aggregate of mineral and other impurities.
  • In electro-refining, blister copper is the anode, pure copper is the cathode, and silver and gold settle as anode mud.
  • Solvay's process uses sodium chloride, limestone, ammonia and water, and heating NaHCO3 gives Na2CO3, H2O and CO2.
  • Copper ore is concentrated by froth floatation using pine oil, the ore particles floating as froth.
  • Drilling of petroleum is boring wells to oil in porous rocks at 500 feet or more, the oil being forced out by gas pressure or air pressure.
  • Petroleum formed from buried plant and animal remains by bacterial decomposition under earth heat and pressure.

Solved Exercises

Exercise Q.2 — Give short answers

Q: i. What is metallurgy?

Ans: 'The art and science of making metals and alloys from their ores with properties suitable for practical uses is called metallurgy.' Most of the metals such as iron, copper and sodium are found in combined state in nature, which are called minerals; an aggregate of mineral and other impurities is known as ore. The basic operations of metallurgy are concentration of the ore, roasting, reduction and refining.

Q: ii. How blister copper is purified?

Ans: Blister copper contains silver, gold etc. as impurities, which are removed by electrolytic refining (electro-refining). The blister copper is made the anode and a thin sheet of pure copper is made the cathode; a solution of copper sulphate and sulphuric acid is used as electrolyte in the electrolytic tank. When current is passed, copper dissolves from the impure copper (anode) as copper ions:
At anode: Cu -> Cu2+ + 2e-
At cathode, the copper ion is reduced and gets deposited over it: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu
The blister copper at the anode dissolves slowly and the sheet of pure copper at the cathode builds up to a large slab. The inactive impurities (silver, gold) settle at the bottom and are called anode mud.

Q: iii. How sodium carbonate is commercially prepared?

Ans: Sodium carbonate is commercially manufactured by Solvay's process. The raw materials used are (i) sodium chloride (NaCl), (ii) limestone (CaCO3), (iii) ammonia (NH3) and (iv) water (H2O). Ammonia gas is passed through a saturated solution of sodium chloride; carbon dioxide gas obtained from limestone is passed into the solution of sodium chloride and ammonia, and sodium bicarbonate is precipitated and removed by filtration. The dry sodium bicarbonate is then heated to form sodium carbonate:
2NaHCO3 --heat--> Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2

Q: iv. Describe the concentration of copper ore.

Ans: The desired mineral from which a metal is to be extracted often constitutes only a few percent of the material mined, so it is necessary to separate the desired ore from useless material before proceeding with other metallurgical operations. Methods used for the concentration of ores are cyclone separation, vibrating method and floatation method. The most important method of concentration used for copper is froth floatation. In this method, the ore is crushed to small size and mixed with water containing a small amount of pine oil. The mixture is thoroughly agitated by passing a strong current of air. The particles containing ore are wetted by oil and float at the top of the mixture as froth, from which they are collected. The froth is washed with water and then filtered to obtain the concentrated ore of copper, while the useless particles settle down in water.

Q: v. What is drilling of petroleum?

Ans: Petroleum usually occurs at a depth of 500 feet or more. The crude oil is found in porous rocks and is often associated with natural gas, which exerts pressure on the oil surface and drives it out through natural openings of the earth. In the case of artificial mining, mines (wells) are bored; this boring is the drilling of petroleum. When the oil pocket is pierced, the gas pressure forces the oil out. If there is no natural gas present in the pocket, air pressure is applied to raise the oil from the well. The oil obtained from the mine is conveyed by a system of pipelines to the refinery for refining.

Q: vi. Draw flow sheet diagram of Solvay's process.

Ans: The flow sheet diagram of Solvay's process (Fig. 16.3 of the book) is described in words with the book's own labels, as this notes format carries text only:
CO2, H2O, NaCl and NH3 are fed into the Reacting tower.
The reacting tower gives two products: NaHCO3 and NH4Cl.
NaHCO3, on heating, gives Na2CO3 (the final product) and CO2, and this CO2 is returned to the reacting tower.
NH4Cl is sent to the Mixing Chamber, where it reacts with Ca(OH)2 to give CaCl2 and NH3, and the NH3 is recycled back to the reacting tower.
In the plant (Fig. 16.2), brine is saturated with ammonia in the salt-ammonia mixer, carbonated in the carbonating tower with CO2 from the kiln, the NaHCO3 is filtered off, and ammonia is recovered in the ammonia recovery unit.

Q: vii. What is origin of petroleum?

Ans: The origin of petroleum lies in plants and animals which lived on earth and in the sea many millions of years ago. These organisms died and their remains became buried under the earth. Due to bacterial decomposition and under the action of earth heat and pressure, these animal and plant remains were converted into liquid hydrocarbons, the petroleum. The gaseous hydrocarbons that were produced constitute the natural gas.

lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Petroleum gases boil below 40°C with up to 4 carbon atoms, while diesel oil boils at 225-300°C with 14-25 carbon atoms.
  • Urea is made by heating ammonia and carbon dioxide at 170-200°C and 100-200 atm, first forming ammonium carbamate NH2COONH4.
  • In copper extraction, roasting forms matte of molten copper and iron sulphides, and blister copper is porous due to escaping SO2.
  • In Solvay's process, CO2 comes from heated limestone and ammonia is recovered from NH4Cl with Ca(OH)2.
  • The fractionating column is hot, about 350°C, at the bottom and cool, about 25°C, at the top.
  • Bitumen is the residue at the bottom of the fractionating column and is made into road coal tar.

Solved Exercises

Exercise Q.3 — Comprehensive questions

Q: i. Describe the composition of petroleum in detail.

Ans: Petroleum: 'Petro' means rock and 'oleum' means oil. Petroleum is present as a dark viscous liquid under the earth. It is also known as crude oil or mineral oil, and it mainly consists of hydrocarbons, i.e. it is a mixture of many hydrocarbons of different molecule sizes. The wealth of a country may depend upon the presence of crude oil, therefore it is also known as liquid gold. The important petroleum producing countries are USA, Mexico, Iran, Iraq and other Middle East countries.
Composition in detail: Crude oil has often been described as a useless mixture of very useful substances. Its components are separated by fractional distillation according to the size of the molecules and their boiling points. Small molecules have low boiling points, are very volatile, flow easily and ignite easily, while large molecules have high boiling points, are not very volatile, do not flow easily and do not ignite easily. The fractions are:
(1) Petroleum gases — boiling point below 40°C, up to 4 carbon atoms; methane for cooking and butane for camping gas.
(2) Petrol and naphtha — 40-130°C, 4-12 carbon atoms; naphtha for lighter fuel, petrol for cars.
(3) Paraffin oil (kerosene) — 150-200°C, 10-16 carbon atoms; paraffin for heating and jet fuel.
(4) Diesel oil (DERV) — 225-300°C, 14-25 carbon atoms; fuel for lorries and ships.
(5) Lubricating oil — 300-400°C, 20-70 carbon atoms; lubrication of machines and engines.
(6) Bitumen — above 400°C, the residue; heated with gravel and sand and made into road coal tar.

Q: ii. How is urea manufactured commercially?

Ans: Urea is probably the most important nitrogenous fertilizer. Its raw materials are carbon dioxide and ammonia: ammonia is prepared by Haber's process from nitrogen and hydrogen, and carbon dioxide is obtained from natural gas (CH4). Urea (NH2CONH2) is manufactured by heating ammonia and carbon dioxide at 170-200°C and 100-200 atm pressure. The formation of urea takes place in two steps:
Step i: Firstly, ammonium carbamate is formed by the reaction of ammonia and carbon dioxide:
2NH3 + CO2 -> NH2COONH4
Step ii: In the second step, ammonium carbamate decomposes into urea and water:
NH2COONH4 --heat--> NH2CONH2 + H2O (urea)
The urea solution is concentrated in vacuum evaporators, which is then rapidly cooled and solidified. In the flow sheet diagram (Fig. 16.5), liquid NH3 and liquid CO2 enter the reaction chamber fitted with a heater; the carbamate stripper separates the unreacted NH3 + CO2, which are recycled, and the urea solution passes on for concentration.
Uses of urea: (i) Agriculture: urea is widely used as fertilizer. (ii) Chemical industries: urea is used as raw material for the manufacture of many important chemical compounds like plastics, resins and various adhesives. (iii) Explosive: urea can be used to make urea nitrate, which is highly explosive. (iv) Commercial uses: a non-corroding alternate to rock salt for road de-icing; a flavour enhancing additive for cigarettes; a main ingredient in hair removers such as Veet. (v) Medical uses: urea-containing creams are used as topical dermatological products to promote rehydration of skin.

Q: iii. Describe the extraction of copper from its ore.

Ans: Most metals are found in combined state in nature as minerals, and an aggregate of mineral and other impurities is known as ore. The extraction of copper from its ore consists of the following basic metallurgical operations:
(1) Concentration of the ore: The most important method used for copper is froth floatation. The ore is crushed to small size and mixed with water containing a small amount of pine oil; the mixture is thoroughly agitated by passing a strong current of air. The ore particles are wetted by oil and float at the top as froth, which is collected, washed with water and filtered to obtain the concentrated ore; the useless particles settle down in water.
(2) Roasting: The concentrated ore is mixed with silica and calcium carbonate and is heated in a blast furnace; matte is formed, which consists of molten copper and iron sulphides.
(3) Reduction: The matte is heated in a Bessemer converter and air is blown through the molten copper sulphide, which is converted into elemental copper:
Cu2S + O2 -> 2Cu + SO2
The elemental copper is poured into moulds where it is cooled. It is now called blister copper, because it has a porous surface due to the escape of SO2 gas during solidification.
(4) Electro-refining: Blister copper contains silver, gold etc. as impurities, which are removed by electrolytic refining. Blister copper is made the anode and a thin sheet of pure copper the cathode, in a solution of copper sulphate and sulphuric acid. At the anode: Cu -> Cu2+ + 2e-; at the cathode: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu. Pure copper builds up at the cathode, and the inactive impurities (silver, gold) settle at the bottom as anode mud.

Q: iv. Describe in detail the Solvay's process.

Ans: Sodium carbonate is one of the most important chemicals; it is used in the manufacture of glass, paper and textiles, and in laundering. It is commercially manufactured by Solvay's process.
Raw materials: (i) sodium chloride (NaCl), (ii) limestone (CaCO3), (iii) ammonia (NH3) and (iv) water (H2O).
Main process and basic reactions: Ammonia gas is passed through a saturated solution of sodium chloride in a saturating tank, so the sodium chloride gets saturated with ammonia. Carbon dioxide gas obtained from limestone is passed into the solution of sodium chloride and ammonia. The series of reactions involved is:
CaCO3 --heat--> CaO + CO2
NH3 + H2O + CO2 -> NH4+ + HCO3-
NH4+ + HCO3- + Na+ + Cl- -> NaHCO3 + NH4Cl
Sodium bicarbonate is precipitated and removed by filtration. The dry sodium bicarbonate is then heated to form sodium carbonate:
2NaHCO3 --heat--> Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2
The efficiency of the process is increased by treating the ammonium chloride (NH4Cl) solution with calcium hydroxide; ammonia is recovered and is allowed to enter the process again and again:
Ca(OH)2 + 2NH4Cl -> CaCl2 + 2H2O + 2NH3
The carbon dioxide evolved upon heating the sodium bicarbonate is also returned to the process, as shown in the flow sheet: CO2, H2O, NaCl and NH3 enter the reacting tower; NaHCO3 and NH4Cl are formed; NaHCO3 gives Na2CO3 and CO2 (recycled), and NH4Cl with Ca(OH)2 in the mixing chamber gives CaCl2 and NH3 (recycled).

Q: v. Define fractional distillation. How fractional distillation is carried out in petroleum?

Ans: Fractional distillation is the process in which the different fractions of a mixture like petroleum are separated according to the difference in their boiling points. The conversion of crude oil into useful products is called refining, which is carried out in a fractionating column.
How it is carried out in petroleum: The petroleum is heated above 400°C in a furnace. The vapours of petroleum, under high pressure, are carried to the fractionating column. The column is divided into several compartments, each of which has a specific range of temperature (hot, about 350°C, at the bottom and cool, about 25°C, at the top). As the petroleum vapours rise up in the column, they condense and separate out into several fractions: refinery gases at the top (bottled gas), then gasoline (petrol, fuel for cars), naphtha (making chemicals), kerosene (aircraft fuel), diesel oil (fuel for cars, lorries and buses), fuel oil (fuel for ships and power stations), and the residue (bitumen for roads and roofs) at the bottom.
The important fractions with their boiling points, molecule sizes and uses are: petroleum gases (below 40°C, up to 4 carbon atoms; methane for cooking, butane for camping gas); petrol and naphtha (40-130°C, 4-12 carbon atoms; naphtha for lighter fuel, petrol for cars); paraffin oil/kerosene (150-200°C, 10-16 carbon atoms; heating and jet fuel); diesel oil (225-300°C, 14-25 carbon atoms; fuel for lorries and ships); lubricating oil (300-400°C, 20-70 carbon atoms; lubrication of machines and engines); bitumen (above 400°C, residue; heated with gravel and sand and made into road coal tar).
